The rejection of "a manifest file found by walking up from the entry file"
([`programs/no-runtime-autoload`](programs.md#programs-no-runtime-autoload)) stands, and so does
[`config/nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest`](config.md#config-nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest). Both are about where a declaration is found, and no
declaration is in `package.toml`: a program whose `vendor/` is populated resolves every name the same
way whether the file is present, absent or malformed. A fetched package reaches the program as an
ordinary `autoload` line ([`packaging/a-fetched-package-is-an-autoload-line`](packaging.md#packaging-a-fetched-package-is-an-autoload-line)).

**`[grants]` is the application's grant table** ([`security/grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace`](security.md#security-grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace)).
`nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg fetch` write one line per package in the resolved graph, an empty one
included, and never rewrite a line a person already edited. A person reviews and edits the lines. The
operator's `nvs.toml` can only narrow what they grant. A package's own `package.toml` declares its name,
version, dependencies and the capabilities it requests, split into `required` and `optional`
([`security/optional-capability-degrades`](security.md#security-optional-capability-degrades)); the compiler reads that name and that split for a file
inside the package, and nothing else of a package's file.

**Only the grants fold into the cache key.** Every compiled unit's key carries the grant table and the
capability declarations it is intersected with, the way it carries the extension set
([`config/the-extension-set-is-in-every-unit-key`](config.md#config-the-extension-set-is-in-every-unit-key)), so an edited grant line is an ordinary cache
miss. A changed version, dependency or comment changes no key, because none of them changes what
compiles.

Every `nvs pkg` command finds the file by walking up from the working directory, the way `git` finds
`.git`, and the compiler finds it by walking up from the entry file's directory: a tool locating its
own project is a different question from a language locating a declaration. The file is TOML with unknown fields refused
([`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one)).

**Memory:** the grant table is compile-time input, and nothing of it is held per request.

**Declined:**
- **The grant table in `nvs.toml`.** That file is the operator's and deployment-scoped
  ([`config/nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest`](config.md#config-nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest)). A grant is the application author's decision
  about a dependency, and it changes in the same commit as the dependency graph. The operator keeps the
  ceiling through the intersection.
- **The whole file in the cache key.** A version bump or a comment would invalidate every unit, while
  only the grants change what compiles.
- **Flat package verbs, `nvs add` and `nvs publish`.** They spread one workflow across the toolchain's
  top level, and `nvs update` would sit beside `nvs update-check` meaning something else.
- **`nvs package` as a second spelling of `nvs pkg`.** Two spellings of one command are two things to
  document, complete and search for.

Every `nvs pkg` subcommand is a module under `crates/nvs-cli/src/package/`, which `mod.rs` lists. The
editor reads `[grants]` from the snapshot the runtime enforces, and a route's hover shows them
(`crates/nvs-lsp/src/grants.rs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-fetched-package-is-an-autoload-line`](packaging.md#packaging-a-fetched-package-is-an-autoload-line), [`config/nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest`](config.md#config-nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest), [`config/a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one`](config.md#config-a-duplicate-key-is-an-error-and-so-is-an-unknown-one), [`config/the-extension-set-is-in-every-unit-key`](config.md#config-the-extension-set-is-in-every-unit-key), [`packaging/the-cli-surface-is-novis-own`](packaging.md#packaging-the-cli-surface-is-novis-own), [`programs/no-runtime-autoload`](programs.md#programs-no-runtime-autoload), [`security/grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace`](security.md#security-grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace), [`security/optional-capability-degrades`](security.md#security-optional-capability-degrades).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix"></a>

## Every file in a package declares the package's namespace or one under it, or it does not compile

`rule:packaging/a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix`

Every file in a package declares the package's namespace, `Vendor\Package`, or one under it, and a
file that declares anything else is a **compile error** naming the file, the namespace it declared and
the package it had to stay inside.

A file belongs to a package when it was reached through an autoload root inside a directory that holds
a `package.toml`, and that manifest gives the package's name
([`packaging/a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name)). The check needs nothing more: the package comes
from the layout, its name from the manifest, and the declaration is in the file. It needs no package
manager either, so a package copied in by hand with its manifest is checked exactly as a fetched one is.

Authority is looked up by the enclosing namespace alone
([`security/authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace`](security.md#security-authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace)), which would be worthless if a package could
declare any namespace it liked. This check is separate from the lookup: it makes the namespace the
lookup trusts one the package was not free to choose. A package file that declares `namespace App;` to
reach the application's grants does not compile.

**No fetch-time clash check exists.** A package's prefix is its name, a resolved graph holds one source
per name, and each vendor resolves from one registry
([`packaging/a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry`](packaging.md#packaging-a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry)), so two packages in one graph cannot claim one
prefix.

Hand-copied code with no manifest has no package and so no file check. It has the grant check, a person
writing the `autoload` line that names its prefix, and the audit warning
[`security/an-unmatched-namespace-holds-the-application`](security.md#security-an-unmatched-namespace-holds-the-application) describes.

The file's package is found from its real path: the nearest `package.toml` with a `[package] name`
between the file and the entry's directory. So an autoloaded file, a file a `discover` glob found and
a file a `require` loaded are placed by one rule (`crates/nvs-types/src/package.rs`). The diagnostic is
`E0660`, and a manifest whose name is not `Vendor\Package` is `E0659`.

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name), [`security/grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace`](security.md#security-grants-are-keyed-on-a-namespace), [`security/authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace`](security.md#security-authority-is-the-enclosing-namespace), [`security/an-unmatched-namespace-holds-the-application`](security.md#security-an-unmatched-namespace-holds-the-application), [`packaging/a-fetched-package-is-an-autoload-line`](packaging.md#packaging-a-fetched-package-is-an-autoload-line).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-fetched-package-is-an-autoload-line"></a>

## A fetched package is reached by an ordinary `autoload` line in a committed, generated `vendor/packages.nvs`

`rule:packaging/a-fetched-package-is-an-autoload-line`

`nvs pkg fetch` materialises the graph under `vendor/` and writes **one generated Novis source file**,
`vendor/packages.nvs`, containing nothing but ordinary declarations:

```nvs
<?nvs
// Generated by `nvs pkg` from package.lock. Do not edit.
autoload 'Acme\Csv' from './acme/csv/src';
autoload 'Acme\Http' from './acme/http/src';
```

The application `require`s that file once. **That is the entire integration.** Name resolution is
exactly [`programs/autoload`](programs.md#programs-autoload)'s — paths written as string literals, relative to the declaring file, no runtime loader
([`programs/no-runtime-autoload`](programs.md#programs-no-runtime-autoload)), no walk-up search, no new invalidation edge — and the compiler
learns nothing about packages in order to resolve a name. The proof is structural: `nvs-syntax` and
`nvs-types` gain no package-aware code path for name resolution at all.

**The generated file is committed.** It is short and readable, and every change to the dependency
graph shows up in a diff as a line of source rather than as a change in a tool's behaviour.

The prefix each line names is the package's name ([`packaging/a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name)).
Each package is written to `vendor/<vendor>/<name>/`, its slug as a path, so the folder of a package
does not move when its version does. Beside each `autoload` line, the fetch writes one grant line for
the same package into `[grants]`, an empty one included
([`security/an-unmatched-namespace-holds-the-application`](security.md#security-an-unmatched-namespace-holds-the-application)), and never rewrites a grant line a
person already edited ([`packaging/package-toml-is-a-tool-input`](packaging.md#packaging-package-toml-is-a-tool-input)). The line is the subtree form,
`'Acme\Http\*' = []`, because a package's code is its namespace and every namespace below it, and a
package that already has a key naming its namespace, in either form, gets no line.

`nvs pkg fetch` and `nvs pkg vendor` write the folders, the generated file and the
grant lines (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/fetch.rs`). `nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` write them through the same code
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/minimum.rs`).

<sub>See also [`programs/no-runtime-autoload`](programs.md#programs-no-runtime-autoload), [`programs/autoload`](programs.md#programs-autoload), [`packaging/a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix), [`packaging/package-toml-is-a-tool-input`](packaging.md#packaging-package-toml-is-a-tool-input), [`packaging/autoload-probes-fold-into-the-cache-key`](packaging.md#packaging-autoload-probes-fold-into-the-cache-key).</sub>

<a id="packaging-nothing-runs-before-the-program"></a>

## Nothing in a package runs before your program does

`rule:packaging/nothing-runs-before-the-program`

**No install scripts, no post-install hooks, no build step, no code generation, no macros.** There is
no point in the fetch, resolve, verify or compile pipeline at which a package's code executes. The
first time a line of a dependency runs is when your program calls it.

Most of this was already true — there is no `eval` ([`security/no-eval`](security.md#security-no-eval)), attributes are inert
anonymous objects, the only compiler-recognised attributes are a closed `Core`-owned list, and there is
no macro expander for a package to hook. This rule adds the one thing that was missing, *no build
lifecycle, ever*, and thereby closes the category: the entire post-install attack class has nowhere
to execute.

A package that needs generated code generates it into its own repository **before** publishing,
where a human reviews the output and the digest covers it. The generated file is source like any
other.

A package containing a top-level statement with an observable effect produces no effect from
`nvs pkg fetch`, `nvs build` or `nvs pkg vendor` — only from a call. There is no legitimate exception: in a
language with no FFI and no native compilation step available to userland, an allowance for
"packages that genuinely need it" would exist only to be abused, and if such a need ever appears
the rule is re-argued from scratch rather than amended.

`nvs pkg fetch` and `nvs pkg vendor` read archives and write files, and compile
nothing (`crates/nvs-cli/tests/package_fetch.rs`). `nvs build` compiles a vendored package as it
compiles any other source, and runs none of it.

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest), [`security/no-eval`](security.md#security-no-eval), [`security/closed-doors`](security.md#security-closed-doors), [`security/package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time`](security.md#security-package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-package-cannot-reach-its-host"></a>

## A package ships no `nvs.toml`, and none of its `require` or `autoload` paths reaches outside its own directory

`rule:packaging/a-package-cannot-reach-its-host`

Two things a package may not do to the tree it lands in.

**A package may not contain an `nvs.toml`.** Server configuration is root-owned and
deployment-scoped ([`config/nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest`](config.md#config-nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest)); a package that shipped one
would be asking to configure the host it lands on. Fetching an archive containing one is an error
naming the file, and the registry refuses such an archive at publish.

**A package's files are reachable only from within the package.** A `require` or an `autoload` path
inside a package that escapes the package's own directory — through `..`, an absolute path or a
symlink — is a **compile error**. A package cannot read the application's tree, and the check is the
same canonicalise-and-prefix-check `spawn script` performs against its granted roots
([`security/path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix`](security.md#security-path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix)).

The path half is `E0661`: each `require` edge and each existing `autoload` root written in a package
file is canonicalized and must lie under the package's directory (`crates/nvs-types/src/package.rs`).

`nvs pkg pack` refuses a file named `nvs.toml`, in any case, anywhere in the archive, and
`nvs pkg fetch` refuses an archive that holds one before the package's folder is replaced. Both call
one check, `pack::check_not_server_config` (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/pack.rs`), so an archive from
a mirror or a private registry is held to what the registry's build refuses. The refused fetch
removes the files it unpacked and writes no lock (`crates/nvs-cli/tests/package_fetch.rs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest), [`config/nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest`](config.md#config-nvs-toml-is-not-a-project-manifest), [`security/path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix`](security.md#security-path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix).</sub>

<a id="packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api"></a>

## From `0.1.0` on, a minor or patch release never breaks the public API of the release before it, and `nvs` checks that at publish without running code

`rule:packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`

A package version is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, read literally, and from `0.1.0` onward a minor or patch
release never breaks the public API of the release before it. A major may change anything.

- `0.0.x` is experimental. Any shape may change in any release, and nothing is checked.
- From the first release at `0.1.0` or higher the API is stable. The second part goes up for a minor
  (features and fixes), the third for a patch (usually fixes), and the first for a major.
- Additions and widening are allowed in a minor and in a patch alike.

Package versions do not follow [`packaging/below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left`](packaging.md#packaging-below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left), which is the
toolchain's own scheme.

**A break** is any of these, and an addition that breaks a caller counts:

- removing or renaming anything public;
- a new method on a public interface, or a new abstract method;
- a new enum case, because it breaks an exhaustive `match`;
- a parameter type that narrows, or a return type that widens;
- a new required parameter.

A change the comparison cannot classify is a break, and there is no way to suppress one.

**`nvs` checks it statically, without running any code.** `nvs pkg api` extracts the public API
from the checked program after name resolution, so an alias, an import or a formatting change is not a
change, and `nvs pkg diff` compares two versions and exits non-zero on a break the version step
does not allow. The registry runs the same comparison at publish and refuses the release
([`packaging/publishing-never-overwrites`](packaging.md#packaging-publishing-never-overwrites)). The first release at `0.1.0` or higher waits for a
one-time passkey confirmation by an owner on the website, which shows the exact API being frozen and
says that from then on only a major may break it
([`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms)).

**The guarantee is about shape only.** Behaviour may change in any release, and the reference says
so. Shape is what a compiler can check without running code, and a promise about behaviour would be
one that nothing holds.

**A maintainer who keeps an old major alive publishes a new package**, `Acme\HttpNext` or `Acme\HttpV2`
as they choose, and may set `[package] supersedes = 'Acme\Http'` so that `nvs pkg outdated`,
`nvs pkg audit` and the package page point at it. Nothing requires this. The key is read by
`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/manifest.rs`, and `nvs registry build` prints it.

The check is what keeps [`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum) sound: a minimum is never
a ceiling, so a higher version inside a major must always be acceptable, and the registry refuses one
that is not. Across a major, a break that matters is a compile error, because the whole program is
type-checked.

**Declined:**
- **A new name for every breaking release**, `acme/http` → `acme/http2`. It kept resolution sound only
  by convention, and it charged every maintainer a rename where a checked major does the same job.
- **A namespace depth per major**, `Acme\Http\V2`. It writes the version into every `use` line and
  class name, and asks something of package code beyond its name
  ([`packaging/a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name)).
- **Cargo's `0.x` shift**, where `0.MINOR` is the breaking slot. A version read literally needs no table
  to explain it, and `0.0.x` already covers code that promises nothing.
- **A mark that suppresses a break the author calls harmless.** A check its author can switch off is a
  convention again.

`nvs pkg api` extracts a package's public API from the checked program, without running any of it
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/api.rs`). `nvs pkg diff` compares two versions' APIs, classifies each
change as breaking or additive, and refuses a breaking change in a minor or a patch
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/diff.rs`). `nvs api diff` is a different command: it compares two OpenAPI
documents ([`routing/api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change`](routing.md#routing-api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change)).

<sub>See also [`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum), [`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms), [`packaging/below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left`](packaging.md#packaging-below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left), [`packaging/a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded`](packaging.md#packaging-a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded), [`routing/api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change`](routing.md#routing-api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change).</sub>

<a id="packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum"></a>

## Resolution selects the highest minimum any package asked for, across majors, never a pending version, and nothing upgrades itself

`rule:packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`

Every dependency names the **minimum version** it needs, and the version selected for a package is the
**highest minimum any package in the graph asked for**, across majors too. That is the whole algorithm.

There is no solver, no backtracking and no unsolvable graph: resolution is a walk taking a maximum, so
it always succeeds, it is fast, and it is deterministic without the lockfile — the lockfile records
digests for *integrity*, not to pin a choice that would otherwise wobble
([`packaging/the-lockfile-holds-every-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-the-lockfile-holds-every-digest)). Adding a dependency cannot move an unrelated one,
and the version you get is one somebody explicitly asked for, never the newest thing published this
morning, so a build that worked yesterday works today and a fresh clone matches CI. A graph where two
packages require different minimums of a third selects the higher, and no other package's version
changes.

**A higher version inside a major is always acceptable**, because a minor or patch release may not
break the API of the release before it ([`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api)). **Across a
major, a break that matters is a compile error** naming the package, the member and both versions,
because the whole program is type-checked. `nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` print when a
selection crosses a major and which package asked for the older one. A `0.0.x` dependency is an
ordinary minimum.

**Only a released version is selected.** A version still pending
([`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms)) is fetchable by its exact
version and is never chosen by `add` or `update`. A retracted version is not selected, and resolution
names its fix ([`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted)).

**Upgrades are explicit.** `nvs pkg update <package>` raises a minimum in `package.toml` and shows
the effect on the whole graph; `nvs pkg outdated` reports what is available. Nothing upgrades
itself, which is also why a security patch does not arrive on its own, and why retraction and
`nvs pkg audit` have to be genuinely good rather than an afterthought.

**Declined:**
- **A solver over version ranges.** A range can say "not 2.3.1, it is broken", and every incumbent has
  one. It brings back unsolvable graphs, slow resolution, and an error that blames the user for a
  conflict between two libraries they never read. Retraction covers the one case a range expresses
  that a minimum cannot ([`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted)).
- **Exact pins only, with no minimums.** Every transitive upgrade becomes a manual sweep across the
  whole graph, so a security patch spreads more slowly still.
- **A ceiling at the next major.** It makes a graph unsolvable whenever two packages want different
  majors of a third. The compile error names the real break, and only when the program uses it.
- **A root-only rule for `0.0.x` dependencies.** A `0.0.x` package promises nothing, and the compile
  error already names a break that matters.

Resolution, its crossings and the version states are
`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/resolve.rs`. `nvs pkg add`, `nvs pkg update` and `nvs pkg outdated`
choose only a released version (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/minimum.rs`), and `add` and `update`
print the crossings in their report (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/report.rs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api), [`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms), [`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted), [`packaging/the-lockfile-holds-every-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-the-lockfile-holds-every-digest).</sub>

<a id="packaging-the-lockfile-holds-every-digest"></a>

## `package.lock` records every package's digest, a mismatch is a hard error, and `--locked` fetches nothing the lock does not name

`rule:packaging/the-lockfile-holds-every-digest`

**`package.lock` records every package in the graph** — direct and transitive — with its name,
selected version, source and digest, and with the requested capabilities, repository, commit and
owners that `nvs pkg update` compares against
([`packaging/a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry`](packaging.md#packaging-a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry)). `nvs pkg fetch --locked` and
`nvs pkg vendor --locked`, which CI runs, fetch nothing that is not in the lock and fail rather than
update it.

**A digest mismatch is a hard error** — never a warning and never a re-fetch — and the failure names
the package. The digest is the same BLAKE3 the artifact cache keys on, so a package's identity
([`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest)) and its integrity check are one hash.

**`nvs pkg vendor`** writes the whole resolved graph into the application tree, so a build needs no
network at all. Every `nvs pkg fetch` packs each vendored folder again and compares it with the lock's
digest, and writes a folder that differs again from its archive, which makes vendoring a convenience
rather than a second trust root. A build checks nothing against the lock: `vendor/` is committed
source, read as the application's own is.

The lock is for integrity, not for determinism: [`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum)
is deterministic on its own, and `nvs pkg fetch --locked` on a clean machine writes the same
`vendor/` tree as the machine that wrote the lock.

`nvs pkg fetch` and `nvs pkg vendor` write and check `package.lock` and take `--locked`
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/fetch.rs`).

**Declined:**
- **A digest check of `vendor/` on every build.** It reads every vendored file on every compile, and
  it guards nothing that a person who can edit `vendor/` cannot also change in the application's own
  code.

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest), [`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log), [`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum), [`packaging/an-artifact-is-one-immutable-content-addressed-file`](packaging.md#packaging-an-artifact-is-one-immutable-content-addressed-file).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry"></a>

## Each vendor resolves from exactly one registry set in `package.toml`, by default `https://registry.novis-lang.org`, and never from the first registry that has the name

`rule:packaging/a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry`

Each vendor resolves from exactly one registry, set in `package.toml`, and every vendor not named there
resolves from `https://registry.novis-lang.org`. The client never asks a second registry for a name the
first one lacks.

A registry URL is `https:` or `file:`. `file:` is how the tests and an offline mirror read a directory.
A vendor mapped to a registry other than the default names that registry's verifier key beside its URL
([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)). The client reads the registry's root file,
`registry.json`, from that URL, and the index and archives from the file hosts the root file lists
([`packaging/registry-hosting-is-configuration`](packaging.md#packaging-registry-hosting-is-configuration)).
A private registry is an ordinary registry, so an organisation points its own vendors at it and leaves
every other vendor on the default ([`packaging/a-git-dependency-is-root-only`](packaging.md#packaging-a-git-dependency-is-root-only)).

**`nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` print what a change brings** before a person accepts it: every
capability the package and its whole subgraph request
([`security/package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time`](security.md#security-package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time)), the capabilities that changed since
the lock, the number of packages in the subgraph, the owners and repositories that changed since the
lock, and every major a selection crossed ([`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum)). The
lock records each package's capabilities, repository, commit and owners so the comparison has something
to compare against ([`packaging/the-lockfile-holds-every-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-the-lockfile-holds-every-digest)).

A vendor bound to one registry closes dependency confusion: an attacker who publishes `Acme\Internal`
on the public registry is never consulted for a vendor the application pinned to its own. Searching
registries in order would make the first one that answers the owner of every name.

**Declined:**
- **The first registry that has the name.** That order is exactly how dependency confusion works: the
  public registry answers for a private name it should never have been asked about.

The client resolves each vendor from its one registry (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/resolve.rs`), and
`nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` print the report (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/report.rs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-git-dependency-is-root-only`](packaging.md#packaging-a-git-dependency-is-root-only), [`packaging/registry-hosting-is-configuration`](packaging.md#packaging-registry-hosting-is-configuration), [`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log), [`packaging/the-lockfile-holds-every-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-the-lockfile-holds-every-digest), [`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum), [`security/package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time`](security.md#security-package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-git-dependency-is-root-only"></a>

## A git dependency pins an exact commit, and only the root application may declare one

`rule:packaging/a-git-dependency-is-root-only`

A git dependency pins an exact commit, and only the root application may declare one. Two kinds of
source produce a package's digest, and only the registry kind is transitive.

A **registry dependency** is a name plus a minimum version, which the registry maps to a digest. A
**git dependency** is a URL plus an **exact commit `rev`** — never a branch, never a tag, because
neither is immutable. The fetched tree is packed and digested exactly as a registry archive is, and the
digest goes in the lockfile, so from the second fetch onward the two kinds are indistinguishable. The
clone runs over HTTPS inside a size and a time limit, and its host's address is checked against the
outbound address table, so an internal host is refused.

**Only the root application may declare a git dependency.** The registry refuses a publish whose
manifest names one ([`packaging/publishing-never-overwrites`](packaging.md#packaging-publishing-never-overwrites)), and a git dependency found below the
root is a hard error naming the package that declared it. The convenience of git — a fork, a patch
under test, private code, a monorepo — is a property of *your own* project, and your transitive graph
stays inside registries with a transparency log and retraction: no dependency of yours can bring in
code from a URL you never saw.

**A private registry is a registry.** An organisation that cannot use the public one runs or mirrors
its own, and points its vendors at it ([`packaging/a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry`](packaging.md#packaging-a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry)). Nothing
above changes.

**Declined:**
- **Git URLs only, with no registry.** Nothing to operate, but the transparency log, retraction, the
  advisory feed and `nvs pkg audit` all need an authority behind a name, and every URL in the
  transitive graph would be a trust root.
- **A registry only, with git repositories mirrored into it as named packages.** One resolution path,
  but too rigid for private code and monorepos, and not needed: the root-only rule already confines a
  git source to the project that chose it.

The client clones and packs a root git dependency (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/git.rs`), and
resolution refuses one found below the root, naming the package that declared it
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/resolve.rs`). The registry's publish build refuses a manifest that names a
git dependency (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/build.rs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest), [`packaging/the-lockfile-holds-every-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-the-lockfile-holds-every-digest), [`packaging/a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry`](packaging.md#packaging-a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry), [`packaging/publishing-never-overwrites`](packaging.md#packaging-publishing-never-overwrites).</sub>

<a id="packaging-the-registry-is-a-novis-program"></a>

## The registry service and website are the Novis application `apps/registry/`, and its byte work is the same Rust the client runs, in `nvs` subcommands

`rule:packaging/the-registry-is-a-novis-program`

The registry service and its website are a Novis web application in this repository, `apps/registry/`,
and the byte-level work it needs is Rust in `nvs` subcommands the service runs — the same code the
client runs.

**The application** stores its data in SQLite through `Core\Db`, signs users in with `Core\Passkey`
([`core-classes/passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony`](core-classes.md#core-classes-passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony)), sends push notifications with `Core\WebPush`
([`core-classes/web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message`](core-classes.md#core-classes-web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message)), and runs the subcommands below as child
processes, granted in its own `nvs.toml`. It writes the static index that the client reads (one signed
JSON file per package and one archive per digest) to the stores its settings file names, and where
those files are served from is configuration ([`packaging/registry-hosting-is-configuration`](packaging.md#packaging-registry-hosting-is-configuration)).

**The byte work** is these commands:

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `nvs registry build` | clones a commit and packs and digests the package directory ([`packaging/the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git)) |
| `nvs registry log append` | adds entries to the log and signs a new checkpoint ([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)) |
| `nvs registry log verify` | checks a log directory from scratch |
| `nvs registry index sign` | signs index files with the log key, the time and the current checkpoint ([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)) |
| `nvs pkg api`, `nvs pkg diff` | extract a package's API and compare two versions ([`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api)) |
| `nvs pkg pack` | builds the deterministic archive, as `nvs registry build` does after its clone |

`nvs registry` is operator surface for the service and prints no help in a user's command list. The
`nvs pkg` commands are the user's ([`packaging/package-toml-is-a-tool-input`](packaging.md#packaging-package-toml-is-a-tool-input)).

Running the same Rust on both sides is what makes a digest predictable: `nvs pkg publish --dry-run` and
the registry's build produce the same bytes from the same commit. Writing the service in Novis makes the
registry a real program that depends on `Core`'s web surface, so a gap in that surface is found by the
project before a user finds it. A deployment guide states how to run it, so a private registry is the
same program.

**Memory:** the service's memory is per request, with SQLite on disk. A build or a log append is a
child process whose memory ends with it.

**Declined:**
- **A service in Rust or another language.** It would share no code path with the programs Novis
  exists to run, and its byte work would be a second implementation of the client's.
- **Byte work written in Novis.** Cloning, packing, digesting and log signing are the client's code
  already, and a second copy could produce a different digest.

The application's `README.md` is the deployment guide: the commands that run it and every setting of
`hosting.json`. `NvsBuilder` runs `nvs registry build`, `NvsLog` runs `nvs registry log append` and
`nvs registry index sign`, and runs `nvs registry log verify` when the registry restores itself
(`LogCheck`). The application's tests replace each of them with a double, and
`crates/nvs-cli/tests/registry_build.rs` runs the real service against the real `nvs`.

<sub>See also [`packaging/the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git), [`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log), [`packaging/registry-hosting-is-configuration`](packaging.md#packaging-registry-hosting-is-configuration), [`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api), [`packaging/package-toml-is-a-tool-input`](packaging.md#packaging-package-toml-is-a-tool-input), [`core-classes/passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony`](core-classes.md#core-classes-passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony), [`core-classes/web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message`](core-classes.md#core-classes-web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message).</sub>

<a id="packaging-registry-hosting-is-configuration"></a>

## The registry's hosting is one settings file: stores, file hosts, backup and download logs, with a publish durable on every store before it is visible

`rule:packaging/registry-hosting-is-configuration`

The registry's hosting is configuration. The same `apps/registry/` runs on a developer's machine with
every file in a local directory, and in production with its public files on a CDN; the difference is
one settings file the deployment writes, never a code change.

**The settings file is `apps/registry/hosting.json`,** read when the service starts. The committed copy
is the local one: every store is a directory under the application's data folder, so the whole service
is developed and tested on one machine. A deployment replaces the file. A secret in it, such as a
store's credential or the backup key, is the path of a file, read through `Core\Secret` so it never
prints, and a path that does not exist stops the start and names the path. The file names:

- **the public stores**, where the static files are written: the root file, the index files, the
  archives, the log tiles and the checkpoint. A store is `dir`, a directory, or `http`, where each file
  is a `PUT` to a base URL with one credential header, which is Bunny Storage's API and any WebDAV
  server's. Every public store receives every file.
- **the file hosts**, the `https:` URLs clients read the public files from, in order. The service
  writes them into the root file `registry.json` at the registry's URL, the one file a client reads
  from the registry's own host ([`packaging/a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry`](packaging.md#packaging-a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry)). The root file
  is signed like an index file, and the client keeps the last one it read, so it still finds the file
  hosts when the registry's host does not answer.
- **the backup store**, `dir` or `http`, which is never a public store.
- **the download-log source**, where the file hosts' access lines come from, when the service does not
  serve the files itself.

**A publish is durable before it is visible.** The service writes the archive, then the log tiles,
then the signed index files, and the checkpoint last, to every public store, and answers the publish
only after every store has confirmed every write. A store that fails fails the publish, which the
publisher retries, and nothing a client reads has moved. Why: a client refuses a checkpoint that does
not extend the newest one it saw ([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)), so a
checkpoint a client saw and the service then lost would make the next one a fork. The CDN's store,
off the host, is that durable copy.

**Files are cached by whether they change.** An archive and a full log tile never change, and the
deploy guide serves them with a cache lifetime of a year. The root file, the index files, a partial
tile and the checkpoint change, and are served with one of 60 seconds. The service never purges the
CDN, so it holds no CDN account key.

**The database is copied to the backup store** after each publish and at an interval the settings set,
five minutes by default, and not when nothing changed since the last copy, which a SHA-256 of the
copy tells. The copy is every row of every table as JSON lines, read in one transaction, sealed with
`Core\Crypto::seal` under XChaCha20Poly1305 and a key the settings name, so the backup store never
reads it, and it replaces the one before. It is not a `VACUUM INTO`, because Core's SQLite driver
refuses that statement: it writes a file no `fs` grant was checked for. The log is the record of
every release, so a lost interval loses at most the rows the log does not hold, such as a token
created in it, which its owner creates again.

**A service that starts with no database restores itself.** When the backup store has a copy, the
service opens it, takes the log from a public store, runs `nvs registry log verify`, rebuilds every
release's state from the log, and starts. A new host with the same settings comes up restored, with no
step by hand. The deploy guide stops the old host first, because two services writing one log sign
two checkpoints of one size.

**Downloads are counted from the file hosts' access lines.** When the settings name a download-log
source, a daily job reads the previous day's lines, applies the counting rule of
[`packaging/search-sorts-by-the-readers-choice`](packaging.md#packaging-search-sorts-by-the-readers-choice) in memory, and keeps no line. When the service
serves the files itself, as it does locally, it counts as it serves them, through the same function.
Each CDN writes its own line format, so each source is one parser; Bunny's is the first.

**One host runs each service as its own account.** The deploy guide runs the registry and the
telemetry collector as two operating-system accounts in two service units, so the registry's database
and log key are readable by the registry's account alone. The log key is also kept offline, encrypted,
and outside every store, because a lost key cannot sign the next checkpoint.

**Memory:** a publish holds one archive while it writes it to each store, and the repository size
limit bounds it. A database copy is a temporary file the size of the database, deleted once it is
sent. The daily count holds one day's access lines, twice, and their salted hashes while it runs,
and keeps none of them after it.

**Declined:**
- **The service serving every file in production.** An outage of one host would stop every
  `nvs pkg add` and every fresh build. crates.io moved its downloads off its API servers for this
  reason.
- **A counting redirect on the service.** Every download would still need the service to be up.
- **Purging the CDN on publish.** A purge needs an account-wide key on the server, and a 60-second
  lifetime needs none.
- **Replicating the log asynchronously.** A signed checkpoint lost in the lag becomes a fork for every
  client that saw it.
- **A standby that takes over by itself.** Two writers sign two different checkpoints of one size, a
  fork by construction, while a write outage only delays publishers.
- **A provider's SDK or name in the code.** `dir` and `http` cover a local disk, Bunny Storage and any
  WebDAV server, and the CDN is replaced by editing the settings. The access-line parser is the one
  place a provider's format is code.
- **Hosting settings in `nvs.toml`.** It holds the runtime's directives and refuses a name it does not
  know, and hosting is the application's own.

<sub>See also [`packaging/the-registry-is-a-novis-program`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-is-a-novis-program), [`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log), [`packaging/search-sorts-by-the-readers-choice`](packaging.md#packaging-search-sorts-by-the-readers-choice), [`packaging/a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry`](packaging.md#packaging-a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-registry-account-is-a-passkey"></a>

## A registry account is passkeys and one-time recovery codes, with no email, no SMS, no password, no forge binding and no human recovery

`rule:packaging/a-registry-account-is-a-passkey`

A registry account is one or more passkeys and a set of one-time recovery codes shown once at sign-up,
with **no email, no SMS and no password**, and it is bound to no forge.

- **Sign-up** carries a small proof-of-work against bulk sign-ups. An account can do nothing until its
  first publish, and a publish needs a public git repository
  ([`packaging/the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git)).
- **Several passkeys** may be registered on one account. Signing in is a WebAuthn ceremony verified by
  `Core\Passkey` ([`core-classes/passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony`](core-classes.md#core-classes-passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony)).
- **There is no human recovery.** Losing every passkey and every recovery code loses the account. Its
  packages keep working, and its co-owners keep publishing; the guide advises two owners per vendor.
- **Contact with an owner** is the inbox on the website and the package's public repository.

Every way an account is usually taken over goes through something this design does not have. A
password is phished or reused; a mailbox is taken over and its reset link followed; an SMS code is
swapped to another SIM; a forge account is compromised and its OAuth grant inherited. A passkey is bound
to the registry's origin and cannot be typed into a fake page. Recovery by a human is the step attackers
talk their way through, so there is none, and the cost of that is carried by a second owner rather
than by a support desk.

**Declined:**
- **Email accounts, with reset links.** A mailbox is the most common takeover path, and an address is
  personal data the registry would have to hold.
- **Sign-in through GitHub, GitLab or another forge, or OIDC trusted publishing.** It makes one forge's
  account system part of every package's security and shuts out every other git host.
- **Passwords with a second factor.** A password is still phishable, and the second factor's usual
  fallback is SMS or email.
- **Account recovery by the operator.** A process a person can be talked through is the weakest
  credential on the account.

**On disk.** `apps/registry/src/App.nvs` is the sign-up, the sign-in and the passkey routes;
`Work.nvs` is the proof-of-work, a SHA-256 of a session-bound challenge with as many leading zero bits
as `hosting.json`'s `signUpWork` names, checked once and within ten minutes; `Accounts.nvs` keeps ten
recovery codes per account as SHA-256 hashes, each used once. The schema has no column for a name, an
address or a password. **Memory:** one challenge per visitor in the session, and no state between
requests outside SQLite.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony`](core-classes.md#core-classes-passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony), [`packaging/an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token`](packaging.md#packaging-an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token), [`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email), [`packaging/a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires`](packaging.md#packaging-a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires).</sub>

<a id="packaging-an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token"></a>

## An account that shows no passkey sign-in or reminder answer for 60 fixed days can no longer publish, and token use never counts

`rule:packaging/an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token`

An account must show activity within 60 days, or it can no longer publish; **token use never counts as
activity**. The 60 days are fixed and are not a setting. The account's packages stay available, and its
releases are untouched.

**Activity is one of two things:**

- **A passkey sign-in** ([`packaging/a-registry-account-is-a-passkey`](packaging.md#packaging-a-registry-account-is-a-passkey)).
- **The "Yes, I am here" answer to a reminder.** A Web Push reminder carries a one-time code inside its
  encrypted payload, and the action button, or the notification itself through a small page, sends that
  code back. A webhook reminder carries a one-time "I am here" link that counts the same way, so an
  owner whose only channel is a webhook can answer too
  ([`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email)).

**An answer keeps an active account active, and cannot revive a lapsed one.** After 60 days without
activity, only a passkey sign-in makes the account active again. The owner chooses when reminders start,
such as after 14, 30 or 45 quiet days.

A token lives in CI and is the credential most likely to leak, and an account kept alive by its own
token would stay able to publish long after its owner stopped looking. The rule ties publishing to a
person who answered recently. The answer to a reminder needs the device that holds the push
subscription or the channel the owner verified, which a leaked token does not give, and a lapsed
account needs the passkey itself.

**Declined:**
- **Counting a publish or any token use as activity.** A stolen token would then keep the account it
  was stolen from active forever.
- **A period the owner sets.** The 60 days are a bound on how long a leaked token stays useful, and a
  bound that each owner can raise is not one.

**On disk** in `apps/registry/src/Activity.nvs`. `accounts.active_at` is the last activity, and
`Publish` refuses an account whose `active_at` is 60 days old. The owner picks the first reminder
from 7 to 59 quiet days (30 until they choose, `POST /api/account/reminders`), and an account that
does not answer gets another every 7 days until it lapses. The daily job sends them through
`Notices::tell`. Each reminder has a new one-time code, stored as a hash, that works until the account
would lapse and only once. A push message carries it as `here` in its encrypted payload; a webhook
message is `{"type": "reminder", "link": "<origin>/here/<code>"}`. `GET /here/<code>` is the small
page with the "Yes, I am here" button, and only its `POST` counts, so a link preview that opens the
page counts nothing. **Memory:** one row per account that set a reminder or got one.

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-registry-account-is-a-passkey`](packaging.md#packaging-a-registry-account-is-a-passkey), [`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email), [`packaging/a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires`](packaging.md#packaging-a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires).</sub>

<a id="packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email"></a>

## Every owner is notified of each publish, token, owner change, unlist and retraction through Web Push or a webhook they verified, and an account with no verified channel cannot publish

`rule:packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`

Every owner is notified of each publish, new token, owner change, unlist and retraction through the
channels that owner set up — **Web Push** and **webhooks** — and an account with no verified channel
cannot publish and cannot be added as an owner.

**The channels an owner sets up:**

- **Web Push**, one click in the browser. Each message is sent through `Core\WebPush`
  ([`core-classes/web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message`](core-classes.md#core-classes-web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message)), encrypted to the device and signed with the
  registry's VAPID key. An owner may register any number of devices. A device is added only while signed
  in with a passkey, and adding or removing one notifies every other device and webhook of that account.
  A subscription the push service reports gone is dropped, and the account page lists each device with
  the date it last answered.
- **Webhooks**: a signed POST to a URL the owner gives, such as ntfy, Matrix, Discord or the owner's own
  server. It is sent through the outbound address table, so an internal host is refused, and it is
  retried. Each message also carries a one-time "I am here" link
  ([`packaging/an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token`](packaging.md#packaging-an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token)).

**Always present, whatever the owner set up:** a signed feed per vendor, the inbox on the website, and
`nvs pkg publish` and `nvs pkg whoami` printing the pending releases the caller did not confirm. A
public feed lists every pending release ([`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms)).
`nvs pkg publish` warns when no device or webhook of an owner of the vendor took the message.

**One message per event, saved with the change.** Each change writes a `notices` row in the
transaction that writes the change and its log entry, so an event is never shown without its message.
The route sends every unsent row once it commits, and claims each row before it sends it, so two
requests never send one message twice. The every-minute job sends what a failed request left. A message
goes to every owner of the vendor and to the account the event is about, such as a removed owner or the
maker of a token.

**The feeds are C2SP signed notes under the log's key**, the format of the log's checkpoints:
`GET /feeds/vendors/<vendor>` has the newest 100 events and `GET /feeds/pending` every pending release.
Each line after the name and the count is one JSON object. The log's public key checks a feed, with the
client's note reader or any C2SP library. So a copy of a feed can be checked, wherever it came from. The
inbox, `GET /api/inbox`, is the same rows for a signed-in account.

**A verified channel is mandatory.** A push device is verified by the action on a test push, which
sends back the one-time code inside the encrypted payload. A webhook is verified by a one-time code the
registry sends to it, which the owner returns on the website or through the link in the message. **A
channel that stops working stops counting**: the push service reports it gone, or a webhook still fails
after its retries. An account whose last channel fails cannot publish until it verifies one again.

The seven-day window protects a vendor only if somebody hears about the release inside it, so a channel
that reaches a person is part of the right to publish. Adding a device needs a passkey, and every other
channel hears about it, so an attacker cannot quietly add a device of their own to receive the codes.

**Memory:** the service holds one message per send while it encrypts and posts it; subscriptions,
webhooks and one short row per event are on disk. A pending list checks the newest 500 releases no
owner confirmed, so a request's work stays bounded as the registry grows.

**Declined:**
- **Email.** The registry holds no address ([`packaging/a-registry-account-is-a-passkey`](packaging.md#packaging-a-registry-account-is-a-passkey)), and a
  mailbox is a takeover path.
- **Notification as an option an owner may skip.** An owner nobody can reach makes the pending window
  worthless for that vendor.
- **An Atom or RSS feed.** A feed reader cannot check a signature, and a second key only for feeds is one
  more secret for the operator. The log's key already signs, and its public key is already published.
- **Sending inside the change's transaction.** A slow push service would hold the database's write lock.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message`](core-classes.md#core-classes-web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message), [`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms), [`packaging/an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token`](packaging.md#packaging-an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token), [`packaging/a-registry-account-is-a-passkey`](packaging.md#packaging-a-registry-account-is-a-passkey).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires"></a>

## A publish token is scoped to one vendor or package, expires within a year, starts with `nvsreg_`, and is stored only as a hash

`rule:packaging/a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires`

Publishing uses a token scoped to one vendor or one package, which expires after one year at most, starts
with `nvsreg_`, and is stored by the registry only as a hash.

- **The scope** is one vendor or one package, so a token in one project's CI cannot publish another.
- **The expiry** is at most one year, and the owner may choose a shorter one.
- **The `nvsreg_` prefix** lets a secret scanner recognise a leaked token in a commit or a log.
- **The registry stores a hash**, so a copy of its database holds no usable token.
- **`nvs pkg login`** stores the token in the data folder under the ownership check the artifact cache
  uses ([`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary)).

Creating and revoking a token are log entries ([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)),
and every owner is notified of a new one ([`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email)). A token
only publishes: a release it sends waits seven days
([`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms)), and using it never keeps the
account active ([`packaging/an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token`](packaging.md#packaging-an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token)). Everything that changes
ownership, the repository binding or a listing needs a passkey.

**Declined:**
- **A token that never expires.** A token copied into a forgotten CI system stays a publishing key for
  as long as the package exists.

`nvs pkg login` reads the token from standard input, never from an argument, checks it with the
registry's `GET /api/whoami`, and stores it under the data folder's `tokens/`, one file per registry.
`nvs pkg whoami` reads it back only after the ownership check passes, and refuses a file another account
can write. Both take `--registry`, the URL a `[registries]` line names, and `http:` only for a loopback
host (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/login.rs`). The service side is `apps/registry/src/Tokens.nvs`:
making a token needs a passkey sign-in in the last 15 minutes, and a token stops when its account no
longer owns the vendor. Creating and revoking a token each write a `token` log entry, which names the
token's id and never the token, and notify the vendor's owners (`Events::token`,
`apps/registry/src/Events.nvs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms), [`packaging/an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token`](packaging.md#packaging-an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token), [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary).</sub>

<a id="packaging-the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git"></a>

## The registry builds each archive itself from a public git commit as a deterministic uncompressed tar, and `nvs pkg publish` uploads no file

`rule:packaging/the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git`

The registry builds every archive itself from a git commit: `nvs pkg publish` sends a repository URL,
a commit, a version and the package's directory within the repository, and uploads no file.

- **The directory** defaults to the repository root, and `nvs pkg publish` may name a subdirectory, so
  one repository can hold several packages.
- **The clone** is `nvs registry build`, which fetches that commit over HTTPS from any git host through
  `gix`, inside a time limit and a 512 MiB size limit. It fetches that commit alone, with no history,
  so a repository's past never counts against a package. Its host's address is checked against the
  outbound address table, so an internal host is refused. The clone is larger than the archive limit
  because one repository may hold several packages and the files around them.
- **The archive** is an uncompressed `ustar` tar of the files
  [`packaging/a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists) names, sorted by path bytes,
  with every time, owner and mode field fixed and no link or special file. Its BLAKE3 digest is the
  package's identity ([`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest)). A transport may compress it.
- **The repository URL is bound at the package's first publish.** Changing it needs a passkey, is a log
  entry, and notifies every owner.
- **`nvs pkg publish --dry-run` runs the same packing locally**, so a publisher can predict the digest
  before sending anything. The client's `nvs pkg pack` and the registry's build run the same code
  ([`packaging/the-registry-is-a-novis-program`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-is-a-novis-program)).

The commit each version was built from is public on the package page, so anybody can read exactly the
source the digest covers. An uploaded file has no such tie: it can contain code that is in no
repository, which is how a release built on a compromised laptop carries what its source does not. A
build the registry does itself makes the public commit and the published bytes one thing.

**Memory:** a build holds one clone, inside its size limit, on disk while it packs. Nothing of it is
held after the digest is recorded.

**Declined:**
- **An uploaded archive.** The bytes would be whatever the publisher's machine produced, with nothing
  linking them to any reviewable source.
- **Binding a package to a forge,** through forge sign-in or OIDC trusted publishing. Any git host
  over HTTPS works, and no forge's account system becomes part of the registry's security
  ([`packaging/a-registry-account-is-a-passkey`](packaging.md#packaging-a-registry-account-is-a-passkey)).
- **A compressed archive as the identity.** Compression output differs between library versions; the
  uncompressed tar is the same bytes on every machine.

**On disk.** `nvs registry build` (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/build.rs`) clones, packs and digests,
and the service runs it through `Registry\Builder` for every publish (`apps/registry/src/Publish.nvs`).
The service binds the repository URL and the directory at the first publish, and refuses a publish
from another repository. An owner who signed in with a passkey in the last 15 minutes moves the
package with `POST /api/packages/<vendor>/<name>/repository` (`App::rebind`), which writes a
`repository` log entry and notifies the vendor's owners (`Events::repository`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest), [`packaging/a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists), [`packaging/publishing-never-overwrites`](packaging.md#packaging-publishing-never-overwrites), [`packaging/the-registry-is-a-novis-program`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-is-a-novis-program), [`packaging/a-git-dependency-is-root-only`](packaging.md#packaging-a-git-dependency-is-root-only).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists"></a>

## A package archive carries its `src/` source, `package.toml`, its license and readme, and the files `files` names, within 16 MiB and 5,000 files whose paths work on every platform, and the package reads them without a grant

`rule:packaging/a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists`

A package archive carries every `.nvs` file under `src/`, `package.toml`, the license and readme files
at the package root, and exactly the files `package.toml`'s `files` list names, and nothing else.

- **The root files** are those whose name, ignoring case, is `README` or `NOTICE` with any extension
  or none, or starts with `LICENSE` or `COPYING` (`LICENSE-MIT`, `COPYING.txt`). Only the package
  root is searched. **A package with no license file is refused** by `nvs pkg pack` and at publish.
- **`files`** is a list of exact paths relative to the package root: no glob, no directory. Each must
  be a regular file at the commit, or the pack fails naming it. A path ending in `.nvs`, and a path the
  default set already carries, is refused, so every line of code arrives through the autoload root,
  where [`packaging/a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix) checks it. A `.nvsx` component,
  a font, a template or a data table is listed here.
- **The limits:** the files' sizes add up to at most **16 MiB**, and the archive holds at most
  **5,000** files. Both are constants of the archive format, shared by `nvs pkg pack`, the registry's
  build and the fetch, and neither has a setting. A file too large for them is an external download
  ([`packaging/an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size`](packaging.md#packaging-an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size)).
- **Every path works on every platform.** It is UTF-8 in NFC, at most 160 bytes, and no two paths are
  equal ignoring case. No component is a name Windows reserves (`CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `COM1` to
  `COM9`, `LPT1` to `LPT9`, with any extension), contains a control character or one of `<>:"\|?*`, or
  ends in a dot or a space. 160 bytes leaves room under the Windows path limit for the folder a package
  is fetched into.
- **`nvs pkg publish --dry-run` and `nvs pkg pack` print every file with its size, and the total,** so
  the publisher sees exactly what ships before it ships.
- **A package reads its own files without a grant.** Code under a package's namespace may read, with
  any `Core` door that only reads, exactly the files its archive carries and its `[[download]]`
  entries placed ([`packaging/an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size`](packaging.md#packaging-an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size)). The path is
  canonicalized and then compared with that set, so `..` and a symlink do not reach past it
  ([`security/path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix`](security.md#security-path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix)). Writing, listing a folder, and reading any
  other file, including another package's, still need a grant line
  ([`security/package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time`](security.md#security-package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time)).

An allowlist fails closed. With an ignore list, every new file in a repository is published until
somebody remembers to exclude it, which is how keys, `.env` files and database dumps reach a registry,
where they can never be deleted. With an allowlist, a new file stays out until a person names it.
Documentation, tests, examples, CI files and agent instruction files are for the people who work on a
package, not for the program that runs it. The license file is the exception the law makes: MIT and
BSD require their text with every copy, and Apache-2.0 also its `NOTICE`. The readme is the one other
exception, because it is small and a vendored or offline copy then says what it is.

The read gives a package nothing it does not already have. The digest or the hash fixes those bytes,
and the package could carry the same bytes as a string constant in its source. A grant for it would
name a folder that changes with every version, and an application author asked for one on every
package with a font or a template learns to grant broad file access, which is the habit the grant
lines exist to prevent. The set is the listed files and not the package's folder, because an
application may put its own files there.

The limits are counted on the files, not on a compressed archive: compression is the transport's
([`packaging/the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git)), source compresses five to ten times while
a font or an image barely compresses, and a publisher predicts the exact figure locally. 16 MiB is
several times a large framework's source. A limit can be raised but never lowered, because a published
version is immutable ([`packaging/publishing-never-overwrites`](packaging.md#packaging-publishing-never-overwrites)): raising one ships in a client
release first, and an older client refuses a larger archive with a message naming the update.

**The fetch enforces the same limits while it reads.** It stops at one byte past the largest archive
the two limits allow, before the digest is checked, so a hostile mirror cannot fill a disk or memory
with an archive the digest would have refused afterwards.

**Memory:** the pack and the fetch stream the archive to and from disk, so memory does not grow with
it. The read check holds one set of paths per fetched package for the life of the process, and
nothing per request.

**Declined:**
- **An ignore list** (`.npmignore`, `exclude`). It fails open.
- **A glob or a directory in `files`.** Either picks up whatever is added to the repository later, which
  is the ignore list again.
- **Every `.md` file by default.** It ships `docs/` trees, contributor guides and agent instruction
  files to every installer, and a markdown file under `tests/` with them.
- **A changelog in the default set.** It grows with every release, so every version would ship the
  whole history again. The package page links the commit each version was built from.
- **A limit on the compressed size.** It gives source a hidden five- to tenfold allowance over assets,
  and no publisher can predict it exactly.
- **A grant line for a package to read its own files.** It is friction with no security in it, and
  it trains authors to grant more than that.
- **The whole package folder readable without a grant.** An application's own files placed there
  would become readable by the package.
- **A larger limit raised per package on request.** It needs a person to decide each request, and the
  operator only withholds ([`packaging/the-operator-only-withholds`](packaging.md#packaging-the-operator-only-withholds)).

`nvs pkg pack` builds the set, checks every path and both limits, and prints what it packs
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/pack.rs`, whose `MAX_BYTES` and `MAX_FILES` are the two constants).
It refuses a symbolic link anywhere it reads, since a link would make the set depend on what lies
outside the package.

`nvs pkg fetch` writes each package's set to `vendor/package-files.toml`
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/fetch.rs`), `nvs_config::package` reads it onto each vendored package,
and the grant check passes a read whose path is a string literal in the set
(`crates/nvs-types/src/capability.rs`'s `own_file_word`, over `nvs_stdlib::registry::OWN_FILE_READS`).
The call carries the word of the file's resolved path (`nvs_config::capability::own_file_word`), and
the read door passes `fs.read` for that one file even where the operator's scope leaves `vendor/` out:
it resolves the path again and compares the words (`crates/nvs-runtime/src/capability.rs`'s
`own_file`). A path built at run time still needs a grant and the scope.

The fetch reads each archive through `crates/nvs-cli/src/package/index.rs`, which stops one byte past
`pack::MAX_ARCHIVE_BYTES` from a `file:` and from an `https:` file host.

`nvs pkg publish` packs and checks the same set before it sends anything, and `--dry-run` prints every
file, its size, the total and the digest, and sends nothing (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/publish.rs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest), [`packaging/the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git), [`packaging/an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size`](packaging.md#packaging-an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size), [`packaging/a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix), [`packaging/publishing-never-overwrites`](packaging.md#packaging-publishing-never-overwrites), [`security/package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time`](security.md#security-package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time), [`security/path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix`](security.md#security-path-scope-canonicalise-then-prefix).</sub>

<a id="packaging-an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size"></a>

## A file too large for a package is a `[[download]]` entry pinned by HTTPS URLs, SHA-256 and size, which the fetch downloads, checks and places without running or unpacking anything

`rule:packaging/an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size`

A package names each file too large for its archive in a `[[download]]` table of its `package.toml`,
pinned by HTTPS URLs, a SHA-256 hash and a size, and `nvs pkg fetch` downloads it, checks it and places
it at its path in the package, running nothing.

```toml
[[download]]
path    = "fonts/NotoSansCJK-Regular.otf"
urls    = ["https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansCJK-Regular.otf",
           "https://mirror.example.org/NotoSansCJK-Regular.otf"]
sha256  = "…"
size    = 16384000
license = "OFL-1.1"
```

- **The package's digest covers each entry,** because `package.toml` is in the archive
  ([`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest)). A host can withhold a file, never change it, and the
  registry neither downloads nor stores one.
- **`nvs pkg download <url> --to <path>`** fetches the file, computes its hash and size, and writes the
  entry. `nvs pkg publish` and its `--dry-run` download every entry again and refuse one whose bytes do
  not match. The registry checks only the form: HTTPS URLs, a 64-digit hash, a size above zero, a
  `license` that is an SPDX identifier when present, and a path that follows the archive's path rules,
  does not end in `.nvs`, is not under `src/` and is not a file the archive carries
  ([`packaging/a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists)).
- **Files are fetched with the package, never at run time.** `nvs pkg add`, `fetch`, `update` and
  `vendor` download them, and a build reaches no network.
- **Every download is HTTPS, and every redirect hop is checked against the outbound address table,**
  at most five hops, so a package cannot make an installer reach a private address or the cloud
  metadata service.
- **The declared size is a hard ceiling.** The read stops at one byte past it, the hash is checked
  before the file is renamed into place, and a mismatch tries the next URL. After the last one, the fetch
  fails naming the package, the path and what each URL returned.
- **Nothing is unpacked and nothing runs** ([`packaging/nothing-runs-before-the-program`](packaging.md#packaging-nothing-runs-before-the-program)). A zip
  arrives as a zip, and the package's own code reads it, with no grant
  ([`packaging/a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists)).
- **A cache keyed by SHA-256** under the data folder, behind the ownership check the artifact cache
  uses, holds each file once across projects and versions.
- **`nvs pkg provide <file>`** puts a file obtained any other way into that cache, when its hash and
  size match an entry of a package in the lock, so a dead URL never strands a user.
- **Everything is shown.** `nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` print each external file with its host,
  size and license, and the total. A host the lock did not hold before is printed as new, and the lock
  records each package's hosts for that comparison. The package page lists every entry.

SHA-256 rather than the BLAKE3 the archive uses: upstream projects publish SHA-256 checksums, and
`sha256sum` is on every system, so a maintainer or a user compares the entry with the upstream's own
list. A package that needs a large file has three other ways to get it, and each is worse: an install
script, which [`packaging/nothing-runs-before-the-program`](packaging.md#packaging-nothing-runs-before-the-program) forbids; a download at run time, which
puts a third-party host on the request path; or a manual step in a readme, which no hash checks.

The cost is availability. A version whose URLs all stop answering stays unfetchable until a user
provides the file or the maintainer publishes a patch with a new URL and the same hash. A third-party
host also sees the address of every installer, which is why the hosts are printed.

**Memory:** a download streams to disk, so memory does not grow with the file. Nothing is held per
request.

**Declined:**
- **The registry mirroring external files.** It would host bytes no commit holds and nobody reviewed,
  and its storage would grow with every large file any package names.
- **A size cap on an external file.** The declared size, the printed total and the new-host notice do
  that work, and a cap would bring back the manual step this rule removes.
- **Unpacking an archive at install.** It brings path traversal, compression bombs and links into the
  installer, which today only writes one file.
- **An `http:` URL.** The hash protects the bytes, but anybody on the network sees what an installer
  downloads and can replace it, so a fetch reads up to the full size before it learns the bytes are
  wrong.

`nvs pkg fetch`, `vendor`, `download` and `provide` and the cache are
`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/download.rs`, the report `report.rs` and the hosts `lock.rs`.
`nvs registry build` refuses a malformed `[[download]]` entry at publish, and the package page lists
each external file with its host, size, SHA-256 hash and license (`apps/registry/src/PackagePage.nvs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists), [`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest), [`packaging/nothing-runs-before-the-program`](packaging.md#packaging-nothing-runs-before-the-program), [`packaging/the-lockfile-holds-every-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-the-lockfile-holds-every-digest), [`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy).</sub>

<a id="packaging-publishing-never-overwrites"></a>

## `nvs pkg publish` names a commit, the registry refuses what the package may not carry, and it never overwrites a published `name@version`
