`rule:packaging/publishing-never-overwrites`

`nvs pkg publish` names a repository, a commit and a version, and the registry never overwrites a
published `name@version`. A version, once published, is immutable; a bad one is retracted
([`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted)).

The caller authenticates with a publish token ([`packaging/a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires`](packaging.md#packaging-a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires)),
and the registry builds the archive itself from that commit
([`packaging/the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git)). **It refuses the publish when:**

- a file declares a namespace outside the package's name
  ([`packaging/a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-file-stays-under-its-declared-prefix)), or the name differs only by case
  from one already taken ([`packaging/a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name));
- the archive holds an `nvs.toml` ([`packaging/a-package-cannot-reach-its-host`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-cannot-reach-its-host));
- the manifest names a git dependency ([`packaging/a-git-dependency-is-root-only`](packaging.md#packaging-a-git-dependency-is-root-only));
- the clone is over its size limit ([`packaging/the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git));
- the archive breaks [`packaging/a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-carries-only-its-source-and-what-it-lists): it is over
  16 MiB or 5,000 files, has no license file, has a path another platform cannot hold, or `files`
  names a missing file, a `.nvs` file or one the archive already carries;
- a `[[download]]` entry is malformed
  ([`packaging/an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size`](packaging.md#packaging-an-external-file-is-pinned-by-url-sha256-and-size));
- a minor or patch breaks the API of the release before it
  ([`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api));
- the version was published before, under any circumstance;
- the account is not active ([`packaging/an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token`](packaging.md#packaging-an-account-stays-active-by-proof-not-by-token)), or has
  no verified notification channel ([`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email)).

A publish that passes is recorded in the transparency log
([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)) **before** it is downloadable, together with
the manifest's requested capabilities, so that `nvs pkg add` shows them before a person grants
anything ([`security/package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time`](security.md#security-package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time)). A release by token alone
then waits seven days unless an owner confirms it
([`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms)).

An immutable version is what makes a digest in a lockfile mean the same thing next year, and what
lets a mirror or a `vendor/` copy be checked against the log instead of trusted.

**Declined:**
- **Overwriting a version to fix a broken release.** Every lockfile that holds the old digest stops
  building, and a registry that may change bytes under a name has made the log's promise false.

**On disk.** `nvs pkg publish` sends the commit, and the service's `POST /api/publish` is
`Publish::publish` (`apps/registry/src/Publish.nvs`). It runs `nvs registry build`, which refuses
everything one commit can show, and then refuses a version published before, an inactive account, an
account with no verified notification channel, a name outside the token's scope or the vendor's
owners, a name that differs only by case, and a changed repository. `Index::catchUp` (`apps/registry/src/Index.nvs`) appends the `publish` entry, whose
digest covers the manifest and its capabilities, before it writes and signs the index file that
lists the version and its capabilities. The publish is answered only after that.

<sub>See also [`packaging/the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-builds-the-archive-from-git), [`packaging/a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires`](packaging.md#packaging-a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires), [`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log), [`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api), [`packaging/a-git-dependency-is-root-only`](packaging.md#packaging-a-git-dependency-is-root-only), [`packaging/a-package-cannot-reach-its-host`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-cannot-reach-its-host), [`security/package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time`](security.md#security-package-authority-is-granted-one-line-at-a-time).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms"></a>

## A release published with a token alone is pending for seven fixed days, fetchable by exact version and never selected, unless an owner confirms it with a passkey

`rule:packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`

A release published with a token alone is **pending for seven days**, and an owner's passkey
confirmation on the website releases it at once. The seven days are fixed and have no setting.

- A pending version is **fetchable at once by its exact version** — `nvs pkg add acme/http@1.4.0` — and
  `nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` never select it on their own until the seven days pass
  ([`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum)).
- **A passkey confirmation** by any owner of the vendor releases it immediately, which is how a hotfix
  ships the same day. The confirmation is a log entry
  ([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)).
- **A release whose dependency is still pending** waits until that dependency is released.
- **A retraction or an advisory sent with a token alone** waits the same seven days, and one confirmed
  with a passkey is immediate ([`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted)).
- **The first release at `0.1.0` or higher** waits for a one-time passkey confirmation that shows the
  exact API being frozen and says that from then on only a major may break it
  ([`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api)). Seven days do not release it.

**A public feed lists every pending release**, so anyone can scan them, and every owner is notified of
each one ([`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email)). `nvs pkg publish` and `nvs pkg whoami`
print the pending releases the caller did not confirm.

A token is the credential most likely to leak: it sits in CI and on disk. The window turns a stolen
token from a silent release into a public, announced one that every owner sees and anyone can inspect
before a single `nvs pkg update` picks it up. A passkey cannot be copied out of a CI log, so a
confirmation with one is what shortens the window.

**Declined:**
- **A waiting period the owner can set.** Every publisher would set it to zero, and a stolen token's
  release would reach every `update` within the hour.
- **Hiding a pending release until it is released.** A pending release has to be fetchable by exact
  version so it can be tested, and it has to be listed so anybody can check it.

The service side is `apps/registry/src/Releases.nvs`. A publish stores the release with its seven
days, and `Releases::selectableAt` takes the later of its own time and every dependency's, walking at
most 16 steps; a dependency outside the registry never waits. The first release at `0.1.0` or higher,
and a later stable one while no release at or below it was confirmed, has no time at all, and the
index writes it as `{"pending": {}}`. An owner signed in with a passkey in the last 15 minutes
releases a version with `POST /api/packages/<vendor>/<name>/<version>/release` and freezes the first
stable API with `.../stable`, whose page reads the API from `.../api`. Each confirmation is a
`release-confirmed` or `stable-api-confirmed` log entry saved with the change (`Events.nvs`). A
retraction sent with a token shows seven days later (`App::retract`), and an advisory sent with a
token enters the log and the feed seven days later (`App::advise`). The client reads both pending
forms from the index, and `nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` choose a pending version only by its
exact version (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/minimum.rs`).

The signed public list of pending releases is `GET /feeds/pending` (`Feeds::pending`,
`apps/registry/src/Feeds.nvs`), and each pending release notifies the vendor's owners. `nvs pkg
publish` and `nvs pkg whoami` print the account's pending releases
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/login.rs`).

**Not on disk.** The website has no page where an owner confirms a release or a stable API with a
passkey (gap:nvs-cli/release-confirmation-pages).

<sub>See also [`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum), [`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api), [`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted), [`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email), [`packaging/a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires`](packaging.md#packaging-a-publish-token-is-scoped-and-expires).</sub>

<a id="packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log"></a>

## The registry keeps an append-only C2SP transparency log of every event it acts on, and a client verifies inclusion and consistency before using an archive

`rule:packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`

The registry keeps an **append-only transparency log** in the C2SP formats — tlog-tiles, with
checkpoints as signed notes under an Ed25519 key — and a client verifies an archive's inclusion and the
log's consistency with the newest checkpoint it saw before it uses the archive.

**What the log records** is a closed list of entry kinds, one per event the registry acts on:

- a publish: name, version, digest, repository and commit;
- an ownership change;
- a token created or revoked;
- a repository binding changed;
- an unlist and its reversal;
- a retraction, and an advisory;
- a withhold;
- a release confirmed before its seven days end;
- a stable API confirmed.

Each entry is canonical JSON with a schema version, and the log is the only record of order.

**The client keeps one checkpoint per registry** in the data folder, under the ownership check the
artifact cache uses ([`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary)). A new checkpoint must come with a
consistency proof from the stored one. An archive absent from the log is refused. An inconsistent
checkpoint is a hard error that names the registry and says the log was forked, never a network error,
and nothing is fetched. `nvs pkg audit` also compares the checkpoint with a second published copy
of it.

**Every index file is signed, and its age is bounded.** The root file and each package's index file are
signed notes under the log key, written by `nvs registry index sign`. The note's text is the file's
JSON, which carries the time it was signed and the size and root hash of the checkpoint it was signed
with. The service signs every index file again each day. The client refuses an index file whose
signature does not verify, whose checkpoint is not consistent with the stored one, or whose time is
more than an hour ahead of the client's clock, and tries the next file host
([`packaging/registry-hosting-is-configuration`](packaging.md#packaging-registry-hosting-is-configuration)). A validly signed checkpoint that is not
consistent stays the fork error, and no other host is tried. `nvs pkg add`, `nvs pkg update` and
`nvs pkg outdated` refuse an index file signed more than seven days ago and name the registry and the
time. A build from the lock and `nvs pkg fetch --locked` select nothing, need only digests and
inclusion, and work through any outage.

The index is what tells a client which version is released, pending, retracted or withheld. A host
that could change it could skip the seven-day window or show a withheld version as released, and one
that could serve an old copy could hide a fix for as long as it liked. The signature stops the first,
the age bound limits the second to seven days, and the lock keeps every build working while the
service is down.

**The registry's verifier key is pinned, never learned.** The default registry's key is a constant in
`nvs`. A vendor that `package.toml` maps to another registry names that registry's key beside its URL,
in the C2SP note verifier-key form ([`packaging/a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry`](packaging.md#packaging-a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry)).

A registry that serves one client different bytes than another must therefore fork the log, which the
next client that checks consistency detects, or sign a statement that contradicts one it already made.
Compromising the registry stops being silent, and the lockfile
([`packaging/the-lockfile-holds-every-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-the-lockfile-holds-every-digest)) then holds the digest so a client need not trust the
registry twice. The log is also why a registry, and not git URLs alone, is the transitive source:
retraction, the advisory feed and `nvs pkg audit` need an authority that cannot quietly rewrite
what it said.

**Outside witnesses can co-sign checkpoints later with no format change**, and none are required now.
The C2SP formats are what make that true, and they are what other transparency logs already speak.

The byte work is `nvs registry log append`, `nvs registry log verify` and `nvs registry index sign`,
the commands the service calls ([`packaging/the-registry-is-a-novis-program`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-is-a-novis-program)). The client's
checks are `crates/nvs-cli/src/package/proof.rs` for the log and
`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/index.rs` for the signed files.

**Memory:** a stored checkpoint and the last root file are a few hundred bytes per registry. A fetch
holds one inclusion proof per archive and one consistency proof per checkpoint while it runs. The
daily signing writes every index file again, one small file per package per store per day.

**Declined:**
- **A log format of the registry's own.** It would work, and it would shut out every witness and
  verifier that already reads C2SP.
- **Witnesses required from the start.** The format leaves room for them; requiring them now would
  make the registry depend on parties that do not exist yet.
- **Unsigned index files.** Only the archive would be checked, and whoever serves the files would
  decide every version's state.
- **A snapshot file listing every index file's hash.** It stops the rollback of one file, but every
  client downloads a file that grows with the number of packages. A daily signature on each file
  bounds a rollback with nothing extra to download.
- **Refusing every command on an old index.** A long outage would then break every build, while the
  lock already holds what a build needs.
- **A time line of the registry's own in the checkpoint.** The checkpoint stays C2SP's, and the time
  is in the index file, whose format is the registry's.
- **The key the registry serves.** Whoever controls the files would then also choose the key.

**The formats are written in this tree**, the exception
[`packaging/somebody-elses-specification-is-a-crate`](packaging.md#packaging-somebody-elses-specification-is-a-crate) allows when it is argued. The tiles, the
hashing and both proofs are `crates/nvs-cli/src/package/log.rs`, on the `sha2` the tree already
links, with no new crate. The only crates for the formats, `tlog_tiles` and `signed_note`, are not
first-class: each is at 0.2 with one maintainer. They also sit on the older `sha2` 0.10 line. And
`tlog_tiles` pulls in `url` and its ICU stack, and `signed_note` a second `ed25519-dalek` beside the
one already linked. That is some twenty crates for about five hundred lines that follow Go's
`golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/tlog`. The code is held to the vectors of transparency-dev's `merkle`
module and of C2SP's and Go's tile paths, vendored under `crates/nvs-cli/tests/fixtures/tlog/`.
The cost is that this tree owns the code for as long as the log exists. The risk is bounded: a
proof's arithmetic is fixed by RFC 6962, and a wrong proof fails against every other verifier.

The registry service under `apps/registry/` runs these commands. `nvs pkg audit` compares the second
copy of the checkpoint a registry's root file names with the log the file host serves, and stops on
a disagreement (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/audit.rs`). The client reads the default registry once its
verifier key is in the binary as `DEFAULT_KEY` (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/manifest.rs`), and reads
nothing from it while that is `None`.

<sub>See also [`packaging/the-lockfile-holds-every-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-the-lockfile-holds-every-digest), [`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted), [`packaging/publishing-never-overwrites`](packaging.md#packaging-publishing-never-overwrites), [`packaging/the-registry-is-a-novis-program`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-is-a-novis-program), [`packaging/registry-hosting-is-configuration`](packaging.md#packaging-registry-hosting-is-configuration), [`packaging/a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry`](packaging.md#packaging-a-vendor-resolves-from-one-registry), [`config/ownership-is-the-trust-boundary`](config.md#config-ownership-is-the-trust-boundary).</sub>

<a id="packaging-an-owner-may-unlist"></a>

## An owner may unlist a package or a version with a passkey, which hides it from search and keeps it fetchable, logged and reversible

`rule:packaging/an-owner-may-unlist`

An owner may **unlist** a package or one version with a passkey: it is hidden from search and listings,
its page says it is unlisted, and it stays fetchable. Unlisting is a log entry
([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)), every owner is notified of it, and an owner
may reverse it.

A lockfile that names an unlisted version keeps building, and resolution still selects it when a
minimum asks for it. Unlisting is not an advisory, so `nvs pkg audit` does not report it
([`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted)).

Unlisting is the owner's way to say "do not start using this" — an abandoned package, a name published
by mistake — without breaking anyone who already depends on it. A broken or dangerous version is
retracted instead, which is what tells the people who already use it.

**Declined:**
- **Deletion by the owner.** It breaks every lockfile that holds the digest, and a deleted name would
  invite somebody to publish different code under it.

An owner signed in with a passkey in the last 15 minutes unlists a version, or every version, with
`POST /api/packages/<vendor>/<name>/unlist` and reverses it with `.../relist`
(`apps/registry/src/App.nvs`). Each change is an `unlist` or `relist` log entry saved with it, and the
index file shows the version as `unlisted`. A token cannot unlist: the request is answered `202` with
the page where an owner confirms it, and `nvs pkg unlist` prints that page
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/unlist.rs`). The client resolves and fetches an unlisted version a
minimum names, and `nvs pkg add` and `nvs pkg update` never choose one on their own
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/minimum.rs`). Each `unlist` and `relist` entry also writes the owners'
notice in its transaction (`apps/registry/src/Events.nvs`). Search counts no unlisted version and
returns no package whose every version is unlisted (`apps/registry/src/Ranking.nvs`), and the package
page shows the version as `unlisted` (`apps/registry/src/PackagePage.nvs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted), [`packaging/the-operator-only-withholds`](packaging.md#packaging-the-operator-only-withholds), [`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted"></a>

## A known-bad version is retracted, never deleted, a token-sent retraction waits seven days, and `nvs pkg audit` names the minimum bump that clears it

`rule:packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`

An owner marks a known-bad version **retracted** with a reason and a fixed-in version, and the bytes
stay fetchable forever. Resolution refuses to *select* a retracted version and names the fix, while an
existing lockfile still builds. Deletion is not offered.

**A retraction or an advisory sent with a token alone waits seven days**, the same fixed period a
token-only release waits ([`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms)). One
confirmed with an owner's passkey on the website takes effect at once. A stolen token can therefore not
retract a good release, or announce a false advisory, before every owner has been notified
([`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email)) and has had time to answer.

**`nvs pkg audit`** reads the lock, never the network's idea of the graph, and checks it against
the registry's signed advisory feed. The feed has one entry per retraction, withhold and advisory, signed
with the log's key, and every entry is also a log entry
([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)), so a feed that hides an advisory disagrees
with the log. For each locked version under an advisory, audit prints the advisory, its reason and the
smallest version that clears it, and exits non-zero while any remain, for CI. A withheld version
([`packaging/the-operator-only-withholds`](packaging.md#packaging-the-operator-only-withholds)) is reported the same way. An unlisted version
([`packaging/an-owner-may-unlist`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-may-unlist)) is not an advisory and is not reported.

**The advisory feed** is `log/advisories` under each file host, beside `log/checkpoint`. It is a
signed note under the log's key whose text is its JSON on one line, signed as an index file is
([`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest)): `"schema": 1`, `advisories`, `signed_at` and
`checkpoint`, the `size` and base64 `root` of the log it lists. Each advisory is `log`, the number of
its record, and `entry`, that record's entry: a `retract` with `package`, `version`, `reason` and,
once a version fixes it, `fixed_in`, a `withhold` with `package`, `version` and `reason`, or an
`advisory` with `id`, `package`, `versions` and `summary`. The
advisories are in the log's order, and a client refuses a key it does not know. `nvs registry log
advisories` writes the feed from the log alone, so its every byte is derived from records the log
already signed.

```json
{"schema": 1, "advisories": [{"log": 7, "entry": {"kind": "retract", "package": "acme/http", "version": "1.1.0", "reason": "It deletes files.", "fixed_in": "1.1.1", "v": 1}}], "signed_at": 1793000000, "checkpoint": {"size": 42, "root": "<base64>"}}

— registry.example.com <base64 signature>
```

**A client checks the feed against the log before it uses it.** A signature that does not check
with the pinned key is an error. So is a retraction, a withhold or an advisory among the log's first `size`
records that the feed does not list, a listed record the log has with other bytes, and a `root` that
is not the log's at `size` (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/advisory.rs`). The feed covers a log that
the client's checkpoint continues, so a record past the feed's `size` is read from the log itself.

**An advisory's `versions` is one range.** `A..B` covers the versions from `A` up to `B` and not
including it, and `A..` covers every version from `A`, while no version fixes it yet. `A` and `B` are
full versions and `A` is below `B`. A second range is a second advisory: there is no list and no other
operator, so this is not the range system dependencies decline. One parser reads it
(`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/manifest.rs`'s `Range`), and the log refuses an `advisory` entry whose
range it does not read (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/entry.rs`).

An owner sends an advisory with `POST /api/packages/<vendor>/<name>/advisory` and
`{"versions", "summary"}` (`App::advise`). The registry checks the range with the same rules
(`apps/registry/src/VersionRange.nvs`) and answers `422` for one it does not read. It gives the
advisory its `id`, `<vendor>/<name>-<n>`, where `n` counts that package's advisories from 1, and
saves the row, the waiting log entry and the owners' notice in one transaction (`Releases::advise`).
A waiting entry has a `due` time, and the log takes it only from then (`Index.nvs`), so a token's
advisory is in neither the log nor the feed for seven days. The same advisory sent again with a
passkey moves that time to now. The package page lists each advisory, and a version's page lists the
ones whose range has that version (`PackagePage.nvs`).

The client is `nvs pkg advise <package> <versions> <summary>` (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/advise.rs`),
one request to that route with the stored publish token, shaped like `nvs pkg retract`. Audit
reports each locked version whose advisory's range contains it (`Range::contains`), with the `id`,
the summary as the reason and `B` as the version that clears it. An `A..` range has no fix.
Resolution does not change: only a retraction or a withhold stops a version from being selected.

Retraction plus audit is the answer to minimal version selection's one real weakness, that a patch
nobody asked for does not arrive on its own ([`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum)),
and it covers the one case a version range expresses that a minimum cannot: "not 2.3.1, it is broken".
If audit proves insufficient and users sit on known-vulnerable versions, the thing to argue is a
narrowly scoped automatic patch floor, not a general range system.

**Declined:**
- **Deleting a bad version.** Every lockfile that holds its digest stops building, and the log would
  record a name whose bytes no longer exist.
- **A token-sent retraction taking effect at once.** A stolen token could then pull a good release out
  of every fresh resolution before any owner saw it.

`nvs pkg audit` is `crates/nvs-cli/src/package/audit.rs`. The service writes a retraction's
`fixed_in` into its log entry (`apps/registry/src/Events.nvs`) and writes the feed again from the log
whenever the index is flushed (`apps/registry/src/Index.nvs`). Resolution refuses a retracted version
the lock does not already have and names its fix (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/resolve.rs`).

<sub>See also [`packaging/resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum`](packaging.md#packaging-resolution-takes-the-highest-minimum), [`packaging/a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms`](packaging.md#packaging-a-release-waits-seven-days-unless-an-owner-confirms), [`packaging/the-operator-only-withholds`](packaging.md#packaging-the-operator-only-withholds), [`packaging/an-owner-may-unlist`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-may-unlist), [`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log).</sub>

<a id="packaging-the-operator-only-withholds"></a>

## The registry's operator may only withhold a version's bytes, for malware or a legal order, as a signed and logged advisory, and never deletes, edits or reassigns

`rule:packaging/the-operator-only-withholds`

The registry's operator may only **withhold** a version's bytes, for malware or a legal order, and
always as a signed, logged advisory that states its reason. The operator never deletes, never edits,
never reassigns a name, and runs no review queue.

- **A withheld version** keeps its name, its version and its digest in the index and the log; only its
  bytes stop being served. `nvs pkg audit` reports it as it reports a retraction
  ([`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted)), and resolution does not select it.
- **The advisory** is signed with the log's key and is a log entry
  ([`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log)), so a withhold cannot be silent.
- **A short published policy page** states this, in words an end user reads.

An operator who can delete, edit or reassign is a second way to change what a name means, and a
compromised operator account would be the most powerful credential in the registry. Withholding is the
one power malware and a court order need, and making it public and signed means every use of it can be
checked. A review queue would make the operator responsible for every package's content, which no
registry can carry.

**Declined:**
- **Deletion by the operator.** Every lockfile that holds the digest would stop building with no
  record of why.
- **Reassigning a name after a dispute.** A name that changes hands changes what every existing
  dependency on it means ([`packaging/a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name)).
- **A review queue before publication.** It delays every release and implies a safety promise no
  reviewer can keep.

The operator withholds from a shell on the server, with `nvs run jobs/withhold.nvs --config nvs.toml
<package> <version> <reason>` (`apps/registry/jobs/withhold.nvs`). No web credential can withhold,
because the website has no operator account. `Releases::withhold` saves the reason and a `withhold` log
entry together, and the index file, signed with the log's key, shows `{"withheld": {"reason"}}`. The
registry's own archive route answers `451` for a withheld digest. Once the log and the index have the
reason, the job deletes the archive from every store and from the work folder (`Stores::remove`), and
running it again finishes a delete a store failed. With a `purge` in `hosting.json`, it then sends
one `POST` to the CDN's purge API for the archive's address under every file host (`Stores::purge`),
through the outbound address check a webhook passes; a failed purge fails the job, and running it
again sends every purge again. Without `purge`, a CDN in front of a store may serve a cached archive
until its cache lifetime ends, as `apps/registry/README.md` says. Resolution refuses a withheld version and prints its
reason (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/resolve.rs`). The policy page is `GET /policy`
(`apps/registry/src/PolicyPage.nvs`).

`nvs pkg audit` reports a locked version that is withheld, with its reason
([`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted)).

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted`](packaging.md#packaging-a-known-bad-version-is-retracted-not-deleted), [`packaging/the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-keeps-an-append-only-log), [`packaging/an-owner-may-unlist`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-may-unlist), [`packaging/a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-name-is-vendor-slash-name).</sub>

<a id="packaging-search-sorts-by-the-readers-choice"></a>

## Registry search sorts by the reader's choice, ranks only on facts the registry witnessed and on downloads, and counts downloads without storing an address

`rule:packaging/search-sorts-by-the-readers-choice`

The registry's search matches text, then sorts by an order the reader chooses: by default a mix of
witnessed work and downloads, and also by date, by activity, by downloads or by name.

**Witnessed work is only what the registry saw with its own clock or measured in the code it built:**
age on the registry, months with at least one release, time since the last release, public API size
(from `nvs pkg api`), doc-comment coverage, and retractions that name a fixed-in version. Git history,
such as the first commit date or the commit count, never ranks, because anybody can write it. The
registry clones only the commit it builds, so it never reads that history, and a page shows only the
repository and the commit each version was built from.

**The formula is one file in the repository**, `apps/registry/src/Ranking.nvs`, whose doc comment states
it in words. Every package page shows every fact the formula reads and links to that file. The aim is
real packages, not one-function helpers, so the facts favour a maintained API over a count of names.

**A package page shows** each version with its state (pending, unlisted, retracted or withheld), the
capabilities each version requests and what changed from the version before, the API diff per version,
the commit each version was built from, the owners and their history, advisories, `supersedes`, and the
facts behind the ranking.

**Downloads are counted without storing an address.** A download is counted per version per day, from
the access lines of the hosts that serve the archives, or as the service serves one itself
([`packaging/registry-hosting-is-configuration`](packaging.md#packaging-registry-hosting-is-configuration)); both go through one function. Only a request
whose user agent is `nvs` counts. One count per address per day goes through a hash with a daily salt,
and the salt is deleted when the day ends, so no address and no lasting hash of one is kept. Copies
from mirrors and from `vendor/` are not counted.

A ranking a publisher can write into a repository is a ranking a publisher can fake. Facts the registry
observed itself cannot be backdated, and showing every one of them lets a reader judge the default
order instead of trusting it.

Search is `GET /api/search?q=&sort=` (`apps/registry/src/Search.nvs`), over SQLite's full-text index
of each package's name, readme summary and doc comments. A query keeps its first eight runs of letters
and digits, so no full-text operator reaches the index. A pending, withheld or unlisted version counts
for nothing, and a package with no other version is not returned. `Ranking::facts` reads every fact in
one query per request, and the package page (`apps/registry/src/PackagePage.nvs`) shows each fact, the
score and a link to the formula. The website's first page, `GET /?q=` (`apps/registry/src/HomePage.nvs`),
is the same search in the default order, with a link to each package page. `Downloads` counts both kinds of download through `Downloads::add`.

A package's summary is the first paragraph of its readme, which `nvs registry build` prints beside
`doc_coverage`, `docs`, `readme`, `downloads` and `supersedes` (`crates/nvs-cli/src/package/build.rs`).
The release row keeps each of them, so a page never opens an archive or runs `nvs`; a release restored
from the log has them null, and its page says so. The release row's `declarations` is both the public
API size the ranking reads and the denominator of doc-comment coverage, so one count serves both facts.

The readme is escaped and shown as plain text. The account page (`apps/registry/src/AccountPage.nvs`)
needs any sign-in, a recovery code too: a visitor who lost a passkey must see the account to add one
and to revoke its tokens, the page changes nothing, and every change it leads to keeps its own passkey
check. A webhook is shown by its host alone, because its path can carry the receiver's secret.

**Memory:** a download count is one row per version per day. The day's salt and its set of hashes are
the only per-address data, and both are deleted when the day ends.

**Declined:**
- **Ranking without downloads.** Downloads are the one signal of what people actually use, and the
  reader can still choose a sort without them.
- **Ranking by git history.** A commit date and a commit count are whatever the repository says.
- **A secret or unpublished formula.** A reader cannot judge an order whose inputs are hidden.
- **Storing addresses to count downloads.** An address is personal data, and a daily salt counts
  unique fetches as well.
- **A `summary` key in `package.toml`.** It grows the manifest for a fact the readme already carries.
- **A rendered markdown readme.** `Core` has no markdown renderer, and one for text any publisher
  writes is a new parser on the request path and a new way to inject markup. It waits for a `Core`
  renderer with its own goal.
- **A cached score table.** The facts are computed per request in one query, O(packages matched); a
  cache waits until a few thousand packages make that cost measurable.
- **A separate search service.** SQLite's full-text index covers a few thousand packages.

The search is `apps/registry/src/Search.nvs`, and the order's facts and formula are
`apps/registry/src/Ranking.nvs`.

<sub>See also [`packaging/the-registry-is-a-novis-program`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-is-a-novis-program), [`packaging/registry-hosting-is-configuration`](packaging.md#packaging-registry-hosting-is-configuration), [`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api).</sub>

<a id="packaging-the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0"></a>

## Until 0.1.0 ships any dependency updates at any time, and the version contract starts with the commit that tags 0.1.0

`rule:packaging/the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0`

Two regimes, and the tree is in the first.

**Prototyping — until 0.1.0 ships.** Update anything, at any time, for any reason. Breakage is fixed
in place; there is no classification step, no absorption ladder, no deprecation cycle, no sign-off,
and nothing to write down beyond the commit message. The contract's rules must not be read as "good
practice to start early" — that is how a prototype acquires a compatibility surface it never agreed
to ([`programs/no-compatibility-promise`](programs.md#programs-no-compatibility-promise)).

**Contract — from the 0.1.0 release onward.** 0.1.0 is the release that first declares the language
complete enough for someone else to write against; which milestone carries it is the plan's to
decide. The switch is thrown once, in the commit that tags 0.1.0, and from then on
[`packaging/the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated`](packaging.md#packaging-the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated),
[`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot) and the ladder behind them apply.

The scheme ([`packaging/below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left`](packaging.md#packaging-below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left)) and the cadence
([`packaging/the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human`](packaging.md#packaging-the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human)) apply in both regimes. The release tool refuses to
plan a version at or past 0.1.0 without an explicit flag acknowledging that the contract begins
there, and the workspace version is below it.

<sub>See also [`packaging/below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left`](packaging.md#packaging-below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left), [`packaging/the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated`](packaging.md#packaging-the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated), [`packaging/the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human`](packaging.md#packaging-the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human), [`programs/no-compatibility-promise`](programs.md#programs-no-compatibility-promise).</sub>

<a id="packaging-the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated"></a>

## A version number describes the enumerated surface, and the Rust crate APIs, the artifact cache, diagnostic prose and MSRV carry no promise

`rule:packaging/the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated`

A version number is meaningless unless the thing it describes is listed. Novis versions **exactly
this**: what parses and what it means; every `Core` member's signature and observable behaviour;
`nvs.toml` keys, their defaults and their changeability classes; the `nvs` CLI's subcommands, flags,
exit codes and machine-readable output; diagnostic *identity* — a code or name an editor, CI or a
suppression comment can key on; the extension ABI a third-party `.nvsx` is compiled against; any
format that outlives the process and can be read back, `serialize()` output above all; and the
supported target platforms and database server versions.

And **explicitly does not version**:

- **The Rust APIs of the `nvs-*` crates.** They share the workspace number as a build convenience
  and carry no stability promise whatsoever; a Rust program depending on `nvs-hir` depends on an
  internal.
- **Anything regenerable from source.** The on-disk artifact cache is self-describing and a format
  change is a cache miss by construction — never a break, never a version event. The same holds for
  a portable bundle, which carries the host that reads it ([`programs/bundle-trust-domain`](programs.md#programs-bundle-trust-domain)).
- **Exact diagnostic prose, timing figures, or the byte layout of anything not listed above.**
  Wording improves between patches.
- **The minimum supported Rust version.** Users receive a binary; MSRV is a build-from-source fact,
  announced in release notes and never a break.

The contract is not in force until [`packaging/the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0`](packaging.md#packaging-the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0) throws its
switch.

**Declined:**
- **SemVer on the Rust crate APIs too.** It would freeze internal boundaries that exist to be
  rewritten, for consumers who do not exist. An external tool built on `nvs-syntax` would earn a
  narrow exception, not a blanket promise.

<sub>See also [`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot), [`packaging/the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0`](packaging.md#packaging-the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0), [`programs/bundle-trust-domain`](programs.md#programs-bundle-trust-domain), [`packaging/an-artifact-is-one-immutable-content-addressed-file`](packaging.md#packaging-an-artifact-is-one-immutable-content-addressed-file), [`packaging/nvs-build-compile-appends-the-program-to-a-copy-of-the-host`](packaging.md#packaging-nvs-build-compile-appends-the-program-to-a-copy-of-the-host).</sub>

<a id="packaging-below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left"></a>

## One `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` for the whole workspace, and below 1.0 the breaking slot moves left

`rule:packaging/below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left`

`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, **one number for the whole workspace**, and the number `nvs --version` prints
*is* the language version. Before 1.0 the breaking slot moves left by one: `0.MINOR` carries breaking
changes and `0.MINOR.PATCH` is always compatible — standard practice, and the only 0.x deviation from
SemVer.

The consequence for anything that assumes plain SemVer is that below 1.0 there is no slot left for a
compatible feature to differ from a fix in, so a "minor" and a "patch" bump agree; and a floating
container tag must never follow `0.0 → 0.1` straight across a break, so there is no bare-major tag
until there is a major. The compatible line is always `MAJOR.MINOR`, and `MAJOR` alone is a tag only
where `MAJOR` is the breaking slot.

The scheme applies in both of [`packaging/the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0`](packaging.md#packaging-the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0)'s regimes; what
a slot *promises* is the contract's, through [`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot).

<sub>See also [`packaging/the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0`](packaging.md#packaging-the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0), [`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot).</sub>

<a id="packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot"></a>

## A change a dependency forced ships as a patch, a minor or a major by who can see it, never by how big the diff was

`rule:packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`

One question classifies a change a dependency forced: **who can see it?** Not how big the diff was,
not how many crates moved.

| The update changes… | Ships as |
|---|---|
| Only Novis's internals — call sites, an adapter, a data structure, a Rust API | **patch** |
| Novis's behaviour back into agreement with its own spec (a bug fix) | **patch**, and the release note names it |
| Behaviour a program could plausibly have relied on, even though it was wrong | **minor**, with the note |
| Anything additive on the versioned surface — a new `Core` member, config key, CLI flag, diagnostic | **minor** |
| MSRV, a build-time requirement, a CI or developer tool | **patch** — no user of a released binary can observe it |
| A removal, rename or incompatible change anywhere on the versioned surface | **major**, and only after the ladder |
| Dropping a supported runtime platform or database server version | **major** |
| A security fix that necessarily changes observable behaviour | **whatever release ships soonest**, including a patch; the note says plainly what changed |

**The asymmetry is the point.** An internal break is cheap and needs no approval — that is what an
implementation *is*. Reaching for a major because a dependency's Rust API changed is a category
error. The surface the table refers to is [`packaging/the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated`](packaging.md#packaging-the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated); the
ladder its last rows send a change down is [`packaging/a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded`](packaging.md#packaging-a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded).
Nothing checks the classification; it is addressed to whoever runs the sweep, and the commit message
is where it becomes visible ([`packaging/one-bump-one-commit`](packaging.md#packaging-one-bump-one-commit)).

**Declined:**
- **Every observable change is a major.** Bug fixes would become unshippable, and a major would mean
  nothing.

<sub>See also [`packaging/the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated`](packaging.md#packaging-the-versioned-surface-is-enumerated), [`packaging/a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded`](packaging.md#packaging-a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded), [`packaging/below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left`](packaging.md#packaging-below-1-0-the-breaking-slot-moves-left), [`packaging/one-bump-one-commit`](packaging.md#packaging-one-bump-one-commit).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded"></a>

## A dependency break that a program author could see goes down a seven-step ladder, and shipping it is the last step

`rule:packaging/a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded`

A dependency change that would land in the last rows of
[`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot) does not go there directly. Work down this
ladder and stop at the first step that holds; every step above the last is preferable to shipping
the break, and the ladder is not skippable because a lower step looks tidier.

1. **Adapt our call sites.** The default outcome, and usually the whole story.
2. **Absorb it behind an adapter we own.** Diagnostic layout is hand-written precisely so the
   language's UI does not shift when a rendering crate does; widen that pattern rather than
   exporting the change.
3. **Compensate at the boundary** so the Novis-visible behaviour is bit-for-bit what it was — the
   right answer wherever the dependency implements something Novis has *its own* specification for:
   regex semantics, decimal rounding, the SQL type map.
4. **Hold the old version, with an expiry.** Written as `# HOLD (revisit YYYY-MM-DD): reason` on the
   dependency's own line in `[workspace.dependencies]`, or as a dated entry in `deny.toml`'s
   `advisories.ignore` for an advisory that provably does not apply. A hold with no date is a bug in
   the hold, and a hold never covers a live advisory that *does* apply.
5. **Fork or vendor.** We then own its maintenance and security response, it passes `deny.toml` and
   the attribution generator like anything else, and it needs the user's agreement before the commit
   lands.
6. **Replace the dependency**, re-running the admissibility questions for the replacement; a swap
   that quietly admits C into the trusted core is not a swap ([`security/no-ffi`](security.md#security-no-ffi)).
7. **Ship the break.** Requires all of: the user's explicit agreement, a deprecation cycle where one
   is possible ([`packaging/a-forced-break-is-announced-before-it-lands`](packaging.md#packaging-a-forced-break-is-announced-before-it-lands)), a migration note
   naming the old spelling and the new one, and a major release to ride on.

The ladder exists because the two costs of a break are in different units: adapting Novis takes an
afternoon, while a program author whose release breaks must audit every file they own. Upgrading a
language must not be a project for the people who write in it.

Steps 2 and 3 mean carrying adapters with no feature to their name — simplicity of the
implementation spent for compatibility of the program, deliberately. A dependency that repeatedly
forces the ladder is a design problem, not an update problem; the hold dates are the evidence.

**Declined:**
- **Never breaking the surface at all.** A security fix can force a break, so the promise would be
  dishonest. Shipping the break is the last of seven steps, taken with the user.

<sub>See also [`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot), [`packaging/a-forced-break-is-announced-before-it-lands`](packaging.md#packaging-a-forced-break-is-announced-before-it-lands), [`packaging/only-a-major-may-break-the-api`](packaging.md#packaging-only-a-major-may-break-the-api), [`packaging/the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human`](packaging.md#packaging-the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human), [`security/no-ffi`](security.md#security-no-ffi), [`packaging/a-c-dependency-answers-two-questions`](packaging.md#packaging-a-c-dependency-answers-two-questions), [`packaging/the-third-party-notice-is-generated-never-written-by-hand`](packaging.md#packaging-the-third-party-notice-is-generated-never-written-by-hand).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-forced-break-is-announced-before-it-lands"></a>

## A forced user-facing break survives one minor release as a warning naming its replacement, and is removed in the next major

`rule:packaging/a-forced-break-is-announced-before-it-lands`

Where a deprecation cycle is possible — meaning the old and new behaviour can coexist for one
release — the old spelling survives one **minor** release emitting a **compiler warning that names
its replacement**, and is removed in the next **major**. A warning that does not name the
replacement is not a deprecation, it is an inconvenience.

Where a cycle is impossible — a security fix, or behaviour that cannot be dual-run — the change
ships immediately with a release note that says plainly what changed, on whatever release ships
soonest ([`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot)'s last row). Silence is never an
option in either case.

This is the seventh step of [`packaging/a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded`](packaging.md#packaging-a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded), and it
is reached only after the six above it are exhausted.

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded`](packaging.md#packaging-a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded), [`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-dependency-move-proves-two-things"></a>

## A dependency move never fixes a guard test by editing its threshold, and it regenerates the attribution file in the same commit

`rule:packaging/a-dependency-move-proves-two-things`

The dependency sweep re-runs a battery whose full order and conditional legs are the sweep
procedure's to state. Two of its rules are not negotiable, and this rule fixes them.

**A guard-test failure in `benches/abi-probe/` is never fixed by editing the threshold.** The guards
encode premises other decisions rest on — no native unwinding through JIT frames, what the sandbox
contains, a coroutine round trip's cost class, the regex engine's linear-time bound. If one fails
after a bump, the decision it names is what gets revisited, and the sweep stops until that is done.
The guards run on all three platforms, on any push that touches a crate whose cost they measure.

**A change to the dependency graph regenerates and commits `THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.txt` in the same
commit.** CI fails otherwise, and correctly: the notice is a licence obligation, not a report
([`testing/attribution-is-diffed-in-ci`](testing.md#testing-attribution-is-diffed-in-ci)). `cargo deny check` and the attribution generator's
`--check` run on every push that can change their answer, and unconditionally nightly and at release
([`testing/ci-lanes`](testing.md#testing-ci-lanes)); they are what make a hold, a vendored fork and this rule enforceable
rather than aspirational.

**`cargo deny` reads every lockfile in the tree, not the root's alone.** The root `Cargo.lock` gets
the whole check: advisories, licences, bans and sources. The eight others get `check advisories`
under the root's `deny.toml`: `extensions/image`, `extensions/intl`, `extensions/pdf`,
`extensions/spreadsheet`, `fuzz`, `tools/covwrap`, `tools/nv-scan` and
`website/guides/markdown-extension`. Licences stay root-only, because what the binary ships is
`gen-attribution`'s to judge. CI's `supply-chain` job and `bun nv ci --check` run all nine, and
`LOCKFILE_DIRS` in `tools/nv/cmd/ci-changes.ts` is the list's home. A lockfile CI does not read can
carry a live advisory nobody sees. Cost: one advisory pass per lockfile, a few
seconds each.

<sub>See also [`testing/attribution-is-diffed-in-ci`](testing.md#testing-attribution-is-diffed-in-ci), [`testing/ci-lanes`](testing.md#testing-ci-lanes), [`packaging/one-bump-one-commit`](packaging.md#packaging-one-bump-one-commit), [`packaging/the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human`](packaging.md#packaging-the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human), [`packaging/the-third-party-notice-is-generated-never-written-by-hand`](packaging.md#packaging-the-third-party-notice-is-generated-never-written-by-hand).</sub>

<a id="packaging-one-bump-one-commit"></a>

## Each dependency bump is its own commit, classified in its message

`rule:packaging/one-bump-one-commit`

Each dependency — or one coherent group that genuinely must move together, such as the `cranelift-*`
crates — gets **its own commit**, with its classification from
[`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot) in the message: `patch`, `minor` or
`major`.

The whole reason is `git bisect`: a bisect across a release then lands on the bump rather than on a
wall of them, and that is reason enough. Nothing checks the rule; it is addressed to whoever runs the
sweep ([`packaging/the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human`](packaging.md#packaging-the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human)), and the sweep's report is where a violation
becomes visible.

<sub>See also [`packaging/who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot`](packaging.md#packaging-who-can-see-it-decides-the-release-slot), [`packaging/a-dependency-move-proves-two-things`](packaging.md#packaging-a-dependency-move-proves-two-things), [`packaging/the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human`](packaging.md#packaging-the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human).</sub>

<a id="packaging-the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human"></a>

## Being current has a schedule, a stale dependency is a defect, and a human fires every pass — never an agent, cron or CI

`rule:packaging/the-sweep-is-fired-by-a-human`

Being current is a standing obligation, so it has a schedule. The schedule is a **prompt the user
runs**, and **no agent, loop, cron or CI job ever starts it on its own** — an automated bump would
commit the one class of change whose whole point is that a person weighed it, and would do so on
the day a release is being cut. Automated dependency pull requests are refused for the same reason:
green CI does not decide a change's classification.

| When | What moves |
|---|---|
| Weekly | `cargo update` within the declared ranges — one commit, one battery run |
| Monthly | Semver-incompatible crate bumps, CI action majors, the developer toolchain, and every hold whose date has passed |
| Within one release cycle of a Rust stable release | The pinned toolchain, in its own commit, green on all three platforms |
| Immediately, ahead of any other work | A RUSTSEC advisory or a yanked crate in the tree — the one item that may interrupt a milestone |
| At each release | The whole battery, the attribution file and the callgrind figures |
| At a major only | The Rust edition, and any hold that turned out to be permanent |

**A dependency more than one minor behind for over 30 days without a hold record is stale, and stale
is a defect**: it gets a hold with a date and a reason, or it gets updated. Being behind is never a
neutral state, because the alternative is one enormous forced migration under a security deadline.
The cadence applies in both of [`packaging/the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0`](packaging.md#packaging-the-version-contract-starts-at-0-1-0)'s regimes.

Staleness compounds in one direction only. A tree one minor behind updates in an afternoon; a tree
two years behind updates under an advisory deadline, across an engine API rewrite, with the JIT broken
in between. Deferring a bump never makes the next one cheaper.

**Declined:**
- **Pinning everything and updating at release time.** It turns continuous small work into a forced
  migration under a deadline, and a guard premise that broke six months ago is found six months late
  ([`packaging/a-dependency-move-proves-two-things`](packaging.md#packaging-a-dependency-move-proves-two-things)).
- **A dependency policy per subsystem.** The premises the guards encode are shared, and a sweep that
  is not one procedure is run inconsistently.

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded`](packaging.md#packaging-a-dependency-break-is-absorbed-never-forwarded), [`packaging/a-dependency-move-proves-two-things`](packaging.md#packaging-a-dependency-move-proves-two-things), [`packaging/one-bump-one-commit`](packaging.md#packaging-one-bump-one-commit), [`testing/ci-lanes`](testing.md#testing-ci-lanes), [`testing/perf-two-mechanisms`](testing.md#testing-perf-two-mechanisms).</sub>

<a id="packaging-an-extension-is-a-sandboxed-wasm-component"></a>

## A third-party extension is a sandboxed WebAssembly component, never a shared library loaded with `dlopen`

`rule:packaging/an-extension-is-a-sandboxed-wasm-component`

Third-party code is added to a running Novis as a **WebAssembly component** — a `.nvsx` file — and never
as a native shared library. There is no `dlopen` path, no `.dll`/`.so`/`.dylib` loader, and no FFI
([`security/no-ffi`](security.md#security-no-ffi)): a component cannot address host memory, so it is memory-safe by construction,
and it runs under the same request isolation, capability checks and resource limits as script code
because the sandbox enforces them rather than the extension author remembering to.

The engine is wasmtime, not a hand-rolled one. The wasm **validator** is security-critical — a bug in
it is a sandbox escape — and it is the same argument that puts `hyper` in front of a protocol parser
Novis did not write. Wasmtime is memory-safe Rust and pins the same Cranelift version the JIT already
uses, so the two coexist with one shared `cranelift-codegen`.

**The engine names the wasm features a guest may use, and turns every other one off.** The set is
WebAssembly 2.0 without `externref`, plus the component model: what `wasm32-wasip2` with `+simd128`
emits for the built-in components and the `nvs ext new` template. GC, exceptions, threads, tail calls,
memory64, multi-memory, relaxed SIMD, wide arithmetic and the component model's async are off. Each is
validator and compiler code a guest could reach, and wasmtime's recent advisories were in exactly the
exception and GC paths. A proposal joins the set only when a built-in component or the template needs
it, and a wasmtime bump that turns a new one on by default does not widen the sandbox. The set is
`nvs_ext::call::PROPOSALS`, and `crates/nvs-ext/tests/proposals.rs` loads every built-in component
under it and checks that a guest using each excluded proposal does not compile.

What this buys: one binary for every platform; bindings generated for any language with a wasm target
rather than C only; a crashing or malicious extension that harms one request and not the process; and
calls that are type-checked at compile time ([`packaging/extension-calls-are-statically-typed`](packaging.md#packaging-extension-calls-are-statically-typed)).
A guest call is a wasmtime async call that the request's coroutine polls on its own core, so a guest
waiting on I/O or yielding at an epoch tick parks that coroutine like any other wait, with no async
colouring at the boundary ([`packaging/a-guest-call-yields-on-its-core`](packaging.md#packaging-a-guest-call-yields-on-its-core)). What it costs is
[`packaging/the-boundary-is-the-cost`](packaging.md#packaging-the-boundary-is-the-cost), and an author who wants direct heap access cannot have it.
That is the point.

`nvs_ext` is the wasmtime host: it loads a component (`crates/nvs-ext/tests/load.rs`) and calls it
under the request's budget (`crates/nvs-ext/tests/call.rs`).

**Declined:**
- **Native shared libraries loaded with `dlopen`.** They give up memory safety and request isolation
  ([`security/no-ffi`](security.md#security-no-ffi)), call `open()` and `connect()` past every capability check, and need one
  binary per platform because Rust has no stable ABI.
- **Rust dynamic libraries over a versioned stable ABI.** They are easier for a Rust author, and they
  still have no sandbox, no capability check and one binary per platform.
- **Extensions in their own process, called over IPC.** The isolation is good, and each round trip
  costs microseconds: two to three orders of magnitude more than a component call, for fine-grained
  work.
- **Extensions written only in Novis.** A Novis package is safe and portable, and it cannot wrap an
  existing C or Rust library, which is the main reason an extension exists. Packages are the other
  half of the story, not a substitute ([`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest)).
- **A wasm engine of Novis's own on the Cranelift it already embeds.** Its validator would be a
  sandbox nobody else audits.
- **wasmtime's default proposal set.** It follows wasmtime's releases, so a dependency bump would
  decide what a guest may run, and it carries GC and exception code no component uses.

<sub>See also [`core-api/five-placements`](core-api.md#core-api-five-placements), [`packaging/values-cross-as-handles`](packaging.md#packaging-values-cross-as-handles), [`packaging/a-guest-has-no-ambient-authority`](packaging.md#packaging-a-guest-has-no-ambient-authority), [`security/no-ffi`](security.md#security-no-ffi), [`security/closed-doors`](security.md#security-closed-doors), [`packaging/a-package-is-its-digest`](packaging.md#packaging-a-package-is-its-digest).</sub>

<a id="packaging-the-first-party-components-are-built-in"></a>

## The image, intl and PDF components are built into every `nvs` binary, sandboxed, and always present under `Novis\`

`rule:packaging/the-first-party-components-are-built-in`

The image, intl, PDF and spreadsheet components are `.nvsx` bytes embedded in every `nvs` binary
and loaded before any `[[extension]]` entry. They are always present: a program may `use
Novis\Image`, `Novis\Intl`, `Novis\Pdf` or `Novis\Spreadsheet` on any host, in any bundle and under
any configuration, and no setting or Cargo feature removes them.

They are still Tier 1. Each call runs in the sandbox with its own instance per request, under the
request's CPU and memory caps, with an empty WASI and no grant
([`packaging/a-guest-has-no-ambient-authority`](packaging.md#packaging-a-guest-has-no-ambient-authority)). The binary is their pin: their digest is computed
at build time and folded into `env_hash` with the compiler's identity. The namespace `Novis\` is
reserved for them, so a loaded extension declaring a class there does not load, and `Core\` stays
reserved for Tier 0 ([`core-api/core-means-always-present`](core-api.md#core-api-core-means-always-present)).

Nothing is paid until a program calls one. The embedded bytes are compiled on a component's first use
in a process and stored in the artifact cache like any other module
([`packaging/a-wasm-module-cache-reuses-the-artifact-cache`](packaging.md#packaging-a-wasm-module-cache-reuses-the-artifact-cache)). What it spends is the binary's size:
mostly CLDR data, the codecs and the PDF engine with its fonts, on disk and in the page cache. The intl
component is ICU4X with every CLDR locale compiled in, and its classes are
[`core-classes/intl-roster`](core-classes.md#core-classes-intl-roster). The PDF component's classes are [`core-classes/pdf-roster`](core-classes.md#core-classes-pdf-roster), and
the spreadsheet component's are [`core-classes/spreadsheet-roster`](core-classes.md#core-classes-spreadsheet-roster).
Should that growth make
the single-file executable impractical for CLI programs, the answer is a smaller locale set, never an
optional component.

- **Memory:** nothing until a program calls a component. Then the compiled module is held once per
  process and shared by every core, and each calling request has its own instance under its own cap.

A build script compiles their Rust crates, under `extensions/` and outside the workspace, for
`wasm32-wasip2`, and packs each with the packer `nvs ext build` uses
([`packaging/nvs-ext-is-the-authoring-tool`](packaging.md#packaging-nvs-ext-is-the-authoring-tool)). `rust-toolchain.toml` lists the target, so no contributor installs it by hand. Because the
crates are outside the workspace, the ordinary `cargo build` never resolves them for the host target.
A clean build compiles all four for wasm, ICU4X's compiled data among them, and an incremental build reuses
their target directory. The one C library is prebuilt
([`packaging/a-prebuilt-wasm-library-is-rebuilt-in-ci`](packaging.md#packaging-a-prebuilt-wasm-library-is-rebuilt-in-ci)).

**On disk.** The image crate is `extensions/image/`, excluded from the workspace, and builds for
`wasm32-wasip2` with `simd128` on. Its Novis source half is every `.nvs` file in `extensions/image/nvs/`, which the build packs into `nvs.source`.
`crates/nvs-ext/build.rs` builds it into `target/ext/`, packs it with `extensions/image/manifest.json`
and embeds it as `nvs_ext::builtin::IMAGE` with its digest. `nvs_ext::load::Loader::builtins` reads
its manifest without compiling, and `Builtin::extension` compiles and checks it on first use
(`crates/nvs-ext/tests/builtin.rs`). `nvs` folds the digest into `env_hash` at start. Every compile
types a program against the built-in manifests beside the entries' (`nvs_ext::load::builtin_manifests`),
and a call no `[[extension]]` entry answers reaches the built-in component, compiled on that first
call (`crates/nvs-cli/src/extensions.rs`), so `Novis\Image\Image::info` answers with no `nvs.toml`
(`tests/conformance/novis/image-info-answers-with-no-configuration.nvst`). The loader refuses a
`Novis\` class from every `[[extension]]` entry. The intl crate is `extensions/intl/`, built and
embedded the same way as `nvs_ext::builtin::INTL` with its digest folded in beside the image's. Its
manifest class is `Novis\Intl\Icu`, and its Novis half is the `Novis\Intl` classes
(`crates/nvs-ext/tests/intl.rs`, `tests/conformance/novis/intl-answers-with-no-configuration.nvst`).
The PDF crate is `extensions/pdf/`, built and embedded the same way as `nvs_ext::builtin::PDF`
with its digest folded in beside the other two. Its manifest class is `Novis\Pdf\Engine`, the
interface `wit/pdf.wit`, and its Novis half is `Novis\Pdf\Document` and `Novis\Pdf\Rendered`
(`crates/nvs-ext/tests/pdf.rs`, `tests/conformance/novis/pdf-renders-with-no-configuration.nvst`).
Its exports are `render`, which lays out and draws a document, `merge`, which joins PDFs into one,
`read`, which returns a PDF's facts, and `read-text`, which returns the text of the pages it names.
The spreadsheet crate is `extensions/spreadsheet/`, built and embedded the same way as
`nvs_ext::builtin::SPREADSHEET` with its digest folded in beside the other three. Its manifest class
is `Novis\Spreadsheet\Engine`, the interface `wit/spreadsheet.wit`, and its Novis half is the classes
under `extensions/spreadsheet/nvs/` (`crates/nvs-ext/tests/spreadsheet.rs`). Its exports are the
writer's, which write an xlsx workbook sheet by sheet, the reader's, which read the sheets, rows and
extras of a workbook, and the template's, which fill the placeholders of a workbook and write it.

**Declined:**
- **Embedded, but removable by a setting or a Cargo feature.** Whether `Novis\Image` exists would
  depend on configuration again, the failure [`core-api/core-means-always-present`](core-api.md#core-api-core-means-always-present) prevents.
- **Installed beside the binary, with an `[[extension]]` entry per deployment.** That is one
  configuration step for features every web application uses, and a program could not know
  whether one exists without asking its deployment.
- **Both finished `.nvsx` files committed.** Tens of megabytes of binary in git on every CLDR or codec
  update.

<sub>See also [`core-api/core-means-always-present`](core-api.md#core-api-core-means-always-present), [`core-api/five-placements`](core-api.md#core-api-five-placements), [`core-api/tier-roster`](core-api.md#core-api-tier-roster), [`core-classes/intl-roster`](core-classes.md#core-classes-intl-roster).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-components-engine-class-is-internal"></a>

## A built-in component's engine class is internal to its component, and a call to it from a program does not compile

`rule:packaging/a-components-engine-class-is-internal`

A built-in component's manifest class — `Novis\Image\Codec`, `Novis\Intl\Icu`, `Novis\Pdf\Engine`,
`Novis\Spreadsheet\Engine` — is called only by that component's own Novis source. A call of one of its
methods, or a reference to one, anywhere else is `E0856`, and the error's help is the class's card,
which names the public class a program uses instead.

The engine is plumbing. Its methods take the records the component's Novis classes build, in the
shape the WIT interface needs, and every one of them is called by those classes, so a program loses
no capability and has one way to do each job. The engine stays in the binary, is loaded and typed
like every manifest class ([`packaging/extension-calls-are-statically-typed`](packaging.md#packaging-extension-calls-are-statically-typed)), and keeps its
`nvs meta --json` entry, which carries `"internal": true`. So does a manifest enum or a source
class's type alias that no public member's signature of the component names, directly or through a
type alias such a signature uses: only the engine takes it. Neither is a feature, so neither is on the proofs roster
([`testing/feature-proofs`](testing.md#testing-feature-proofs)), under `data/proofs/skip/` or on the website.

A file is the component's own when `nvs_hir`'s graph walk added it from the component's `nvs.source`
section: it carries the name `<class>:<path>` and no path on disk, so no file a program writes or
`require`s is one. The check is in `nvs_types::expr::calls`, where a static call resolves its class,
and reads `ClassSignature::engine`, which `nvs_types::ext_lib::seed` fills from every manifest the
binary embeds. An `[[extension]]` entry's class is not an engine: the entry is the program's own
choice and its class is its public surface.

- **Memory:** one card string per built-in component, held by each check's signature table.

**Declined:**
- **A separate list of public classes per engine, for the error to name.** The card already names
  them, and a second list would be a second home for the same fact.
- **Hiding the engine from name resolution.** A program would then get "unknown class" for a class
  the binary does have, and no pointer to the class it wanted.

<sub>See also [`packaging/the-first-party-components-are-built-in`](packaging.md#packaging-the-first-party-components-are-built-in), [`packaging/extension-calls-are-statically-typed`](packaging.md#packaging-extension-calls-are-statically-typed).</sub>

<a id="packaging-a-prebuilt-wasm-library-is-rebuilt-in-ci"></a>

## The prebuilt libwebp wasm library is committed beside its source hash, and CI rebuilds it and fails on a difference

`rule:packaging/a-prebuilt-wasm-library-is-rebuilt-in-ci`

libwebp, the one C library inside a built-in component, is compiled with wasi-sdk by a `bun nv` tool
into a wasm static library committed under `extensions/image/`, beside the hash of the source it was
built from. CI rebuilds the library from that source on every change to it and fails when the bytes
differ from the committed file.

That keeps `cargo build` free of a C toolchain for every contributor — only a change to libwebp needs
wasi-sdk — while the committed bytes stay a function of reviewable source rather than something a
reviewer has to trust. The library runs only inside the sandbox, which is the condition under which
[`packaging/a-c-dependency-answers-two-questions`](packaging.md#packaging-a-c-dependency-answers-two-questions) admits it.

**On disk.** `bun nv webp-lib` builds libwebp into `extensions/image/libwebp/libwebp.a`, and
`SOURCE.json` beside it pins the source tarball and the wasi-sdk release by sha256 and records the
library's own. The build runs on Linux, and under WSL on Windows, and refuses a tarball whose digest
differs from its pin. `--check` holds the committed bytes to their digest, and CI's `webp-lib` job
runs `--verify`, which rebuilds and compares (`tools/nv/test/webp-lib.test.ts`). The image crate's
`build.rs` links the library into its wasm build only, for lossy WebP.

**Declined:**
- **libwebp compiled from source on every clean build.** Every contributor and every CI leg would need
  wasi-sdk before `cargo build` works.

<sub>See also [`packaging/a-c-dependency-answers-two-questions`](packaging.md#packaging-a-c-dependency-answers-two-questions), [`packaging/the-first-party-components-are-built-in`](packaging.md#packaging-the-first-party-components-are-built-in).</sub>

<a id="packaging-an-nvsx-is-one-file-carrying-its-manifest"></a>

## A `.nvsx` is a single WebAssembly component whose manifest is an `nvs.manifest` custom section

`rule:packaging/an-nvsx-is-one-file-carrying-its-manifest`

A `.nvsx` is **one file**: a WebAssembly component implementing the versioned world `nvs:ext@1.0.0`,
with two custom sections inside it. There is no archive, no sidecar manifest, and no per-platform
variant — the same file loads on every host Novis runs on.

- **`nvs.manifest`** is JSON, `{"manifest": 1, ...}`: the one class the extension declares, the
  exported interface it maps, each export's Novis signature — parameter names, types, defaults, the
  trailing options shape — with its qualifier declarations
  ([`security/extension-manifest-only-tightens`](security.md#security-extension-manifest-only-tightens)), the class's `const` members, the settings block
  `[ext.<name>]` it reads, the I/O it requests ([`security/extension-grants-are-an-intersection`](security.md#security-extension-grants-are-an-intersection)),
  the largest linear memory it needs, and each method's help text.
- **`nvs.source`** is the Novis source that builds on the class, as a flat list of
  `(relative path, bytes)`, every file under the extension's own namespace
  ([`packaging/an-extension-package-carries-two-payloads`](packaging.md#packaging-an-extension-package-carries-two-payloads)).

At load the host checks the manifest against the component's actual WIT exports through
[`packaging/a-value-crosses-as-its-wit-type`](packaging.md#packaging-a-value-crosses-as-its-wit-type)'s table, and a mismatch refuses the load. Because both
sections travel inside the component, the `[[extension]]` entry's pin covers the code, the source and
every declaration with no separate hash — which is what lets the loaded set fold into every compiled
unit's key ([`config/the-extension-set-is-in-every-unit-key`](config.md#config-the-extension-set-is-in-every-unit-key)).

The world is WIT and versioned by semver. A host implementing `1.y` loads a component built against
`1.x` for any `x ≤ y`, a minor version only adds imports and types, and a component built against a
newer minor or another major is refused, naming both versions. An `.nvsx` compiled against
`nvs:ext@1.0.0` is not recompiled for a minor engine release.

**On disk.** The world `nvs:ext@1.0.0` is written under `wit/nvs-ext/`, with the WASI 0.2 WIT it
imports vendored under `deps/`, and `crates/nvs-stdlib/tests/ext_world.rs` parses it. `nvs-ext`
reads both sections and parses the manifest and the source list without linking wasmtime
(`crates/nvs-ext/tests/manifest.rs`), and its module doc owns the JSON shapes. `nvs_ext::load`
checks a manifest against its component's exports and the world's version
(`crates/nvs-ext/tests/load.rs`). The built-in components and `nvs ext build`'s output are
components built against the world.

<sub>See also [`packaging/extension-calls-are-statically-typed`](packaging.md#packaging-extension-calls-are-statically-typed), [`security/extension-manifest-only-tightens`](security.md#security-extension-manifest-only-tightens), [`config/the-extension-set-is-in-every-unit-key`](config.md#config-the-extension-set-is-in-every-unit-key).</sub>

<a id="packaging-an-extension-package-carries-two-payloads"></a>

## An extension package may carry Novis source beside its `.nvsx`, under one namespace, and the component's manifest registers exactly one class

`rule:packaging/an-extension-package-carries-two-payloads`

An extension may carry **two payloads in its one file**: the wasm component, and Novis source that
composes calls into it, in the `nvs.source` section
([`packaging/an-nvsx-is-one-file-carrying-its-manifest`](packaging.md#packaging-an-nvsx-is-one-file-carrying-its-manifest)). Everything a program names is under one
namespace, the manifest registers **exactly one class** whose static methods are the component's closed
